questions.subject: Physics

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Momentum 4

Average force equals momentum change divided by stopping time.
Increasing contact/stopping time reduces average force and tends to reduce the peak.

questions.subject: Physics

questions.subject: Physics

At extreme displacement speed is zero and elastic potential energy maximum.
Total mechanical energy is conserved while energy transfers between the forms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Born–Haber cycles 1

questions.modelAnswer: Enthalpy required to separate one mole of NaCl(s). Produces gaseous Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

questions.question: Born–Haber cycles 2
questions.prompt: In a Born–Haber cycle for NaCl(s), give the correct sequence of atomisation, ionisation and electron affinity processes leading to gaseous ions.
questions.modelAnswer: Na(s)→Na(g) atomisation, followed by Na(g)→Na⁺(g)+e⁻. ½Cl₂(g)→Cl(g) atomisation. Cl(g)+e⁻→Cl⁻(g) first electron affinity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Born–Haber cycles 4

questions.modelAnswer: Cycle: ΔH_f =108+121+496−349+ΔH_latt. Sum known terms =+376 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH_latt=−411−376=−787 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Gibbs free energy 1
questions.prompt: Write the Gibbs free energy equation and state conditions under which a reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

questions.modelAnswer: ΔG=ΔH−TΔS. T is absolute temperature in kelvin. A negative ΔG indicates thermodynamic feasibility under the stated conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Gibbs free energy 2

T≈267 K and feasibility above this value.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Gibbs free energy 3
questions.prompt: A reaction has negative enthalpy change and negative entropy change. Explain how temperature changes ΔG and which temperatures favour feasibility.

questions.modelAnswer: Negative ΔG concerns thermodynamic driving force, not reaction rate. A large activation energy can cause a slow reaction. A catalyst could increase rate without changing ΔG.

questions.prompt: For N₂+3H₂⇌2NH₃, the reactants were initially mixed 1:3. At equilibrium total pressure is 150 kPa and NH₃ has mole fraction 0.80. Find the partial pressures of N₂, H₂ and NH₃.
markPoints: Unreacted N₂ and H₂ remain in 1:3 ratio so 7.5 and 22.5 kPa.
questions.modelAnswer: NH₃ p=0.80×150=120 kPa. Remaining pressure=30 kPa. Unreacted N₂ and H₂ remain in 1:3 ratio so 7.5 and 22.5 kPa. Final answer: p(N₂)=7.5 kPa, p(H₂)=22.5 kPa, p(NH₃)=120 kPa

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Write an expression for Kp in terms of partial pressures for N₂(g)+3H₂(g)⇌2NH₃(g).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: In the equilibrium N₂+3H₂⇌2NH₃, the partial pressures are N₂=120 kPa, H₂=150 kPa and NH₃=1100 kPa. Calculate Kp including its pressure units.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: The forward manufacture of NH₃ from N₂ and H₂ is exothermic (ΔH=−92 kJ mol⁻¹). Explain what happens to Kp if equilibrium temperature rises.
markPoints: Raising temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction.
The value of Kp decreases because equilibrium compositions change with T.
questions.modelAnswer: Raising temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction. Equilibrium ammonia yield decreases. The value of Kp decreases because equilibrium compositions change with T. Final answer: Kp decreases when T increases for this exothermic forward reaction

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: For 4NH₃(g)+5O₂(g)→4NO(g)+6H₂O(g), standard molar entropies are NH₃ 193, O₂ 205, NO 211, H₂O 189 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Find ΔS°.
questions.modelAnswer: +181 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: For a reaction ΔH°=−905 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS°=+181 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG° at 600 °C.
markPoints: Convert 873 K and ΔS=0.181 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
questions.modelAnswer: −1063 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: For a reaction with ΔH°<0 and ΔS°>0, explain how increasing temperature affects ΔG.
markPoints: Because ΔS>0, raising T makes −TΔS more negative, so ΔG decreases.
questions.modelAnswer: ΔG becomes more negative with increasing T

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: A heterogeneous platinum catalyst increases the rate of an ammonia oxidation reaction. Describe three key stages taking place on its surface.
markPoints: Reactant molecules adsorb onto the catalyst surface.
Adsorbed molecules react via a lower-activation-energy pathway.
Product molecules desorb, leaving catalyst surface sites available.
questions.modelAnswer: Reactant molecules adsorb onto the catalyst surface. Adsorbed molecules react via a lower-activation-energy pathway. Product molecules desorb, leaving catalyst surface sites available. Final answer: adsorption, surface reaction, desorption

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Explain why the second ionisation energy of calcium is smaller than that of potassium, using electron configurations.
markPoints: Ca⁺ second electron is removed from outer 4s subshell.
K⁺ second electron would come from the inner n=3 shell of a stable argon configuration, so is more strongly attracted.
questions.modelAnswer: Ca 4s electron is further out than K inner-shell electron

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: From magnesium, calcium, strontium and barium, identify the hydroxide least soluble in water and give its formula.
questions.modelAnswer: Mg(OH)2

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: A heavy vehicle travels onto an emergency stopping lane filled with loose gravel and comes to rest. Describe two important energy transfers taking place while the gravel slows the vehicle.
markPoints: Kinetic energy of the vehicle is transferred to movement/deformation of gravel.
Energy is also dissipated as internal/thermal energy of tyres, gravel, ground and vehicle.
questions.modelAnswer: Vehicle kinetic energy becomes internal energy and energy spent moving gravel.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: A vehicle of mass 1.8 × 10⁴ kg enters a smooth emergency stopping ramp at 17.5 m s⁻¹. The ramp is 85 m long and inclined at 25° to the horizontal. Ignoring resistance, determine whether it will stop before the end of the ramp. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻². Show working and justify your conclusion.
markPoints: Equivalent height gained = E/(mg) ≈ 15.6 m or stopping distance ≈ 36.9 m along ramp.
36.9 m is less than 85 m, so the ramp is sufficient.
questions.modelAnswer: Initial kinetic energy = ½mv² ≈ 2.76 × 10⁶ J. Equivalent height gained = E/(mg) ≈ 15.6 m or stopping distance ≈ 36.9 m along ramp. 36.9 m is less than 85 m, so the ramp is sufficient. Final answer: Yes, stopping distance about 37 m along the 85 m ramp.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: In an electron experiment, speed v (10⁷ m s⁻¹) and wavelength λ (10⁻¹¹ m) pairs are (1.5,4.9), (2.5,2.9), (3.5,2.1). Show quantitatively that the observations are consistent with λ being inversely proportional to v.
markPoints: Calculate at least two products vλ, e.g. 1.5×4.9=7.35 and 2.5×2.9=7.25 in common powers of ten.
The products are approximately constant across all three data pairs, consistent with λ∝1/v.
questions.modelAnswer: Products 7.35, 7.25, 7.35 × 10⁻⁴ m² s⁻¹, approximately constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: An electron of mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg travels at 1.5 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ and has measured de Broglie wavelength 4.9 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Calculate an experimental estimate of Planck's constant.
markPoints: Use de Broglie formula λ=h/(mv), so h=λmv.
Substitute to give h≈6.70 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: High-speed electrons strike a fluorescent screen, which then emits visible photons. Explain why individual electron collisions with atoms in the screen support a particle model and how the photons are emitted.
markPoints: An electron transfers a discrete amount of energy in an individual collision with an atom.
The atom is excited when one of its electrons rises to a higher energy level.
The atom de-excites, emitting a photon as an electron drops to lower energy level.
questions.modelAnswer: An electron transfers a discrete amount of energy in an individual collision with an atom. The atom is excited when one of its electrons rises to a higher energy level. The atom de-excites, emitting a photon as an electron drops to lower energy level. Final answer: Electron collisions excite atoms, which emit photons during de-excitation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: A violin string is fixed at each end and is plucked. Explain how the plucking produces a stationary-wave pattern, with reference to travelling waves, nodes and antinodes.
markPoints: Disturbances travel along the string and are reflected from its fixed ends.
Two waves travelling in opposite directions superpose/interfere.
Destructive interference yields nodes (fixed ends), constructive interference yields antinodes.
questions.modelAnswer: Disturbances travel along the string and are reflected from its fixed ends. Two waves travelling in opposite directions superpose/interfere. Destructive interference yields nodes (fixed ends), constructive interference yields antinodes. Final answer: Incident and reflected waves superpose, forming fixed nodes and antinodes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: A violin string has vibrating length 0.33 m, tension 25 N and fundamental frequency 370 Hz. Assuming f=(1/(2L))√(T/μ), calculate mass per unit length μ in kg m⁻¹.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: The fundamental frequency of a violin string fixed at both ends is 370 Hz and its vibrating length is 0.33 m. Find the speed of waves along the string.
markPoints: The fundamental wavelength is λ=2L=0.66 m, so v=fλ=244 m s⁻¹.
questions.modelAnswer: 244 m s⁻¹

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: A resistance wire is wound in 50 turns around a non-conducting cylinder of diameter 8.0 mm. Its total resistance is 250 Ω and resistivity is 4.2 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. Neglecting wire pitch, calculate wire cross-sectional area.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: A 250 Ω resistor rated at maximum power 0.36 W is connected in a 9.0 V circuit. Assess whether the resistor is safely rated even if the entire 9.0 V were across it. Give a calculation and conclusion.
markPoints: Maximum conceivable power is V²/R=9.0²/250=0.324 W.
0.324 W is below 0.36 W, so the resistor is adequately rated.
questions.modelAnswer: 0.324 W < 0.36 W, therefore the resistor is suitable.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.prompt: A thermistor with a negative temperature coefficient is connected as the lower element of a potential divider, and the output p.d. is measured across it. Explain how increasing temperature changes this output.
markPoints: Thermistor resistance decreases as temperature increases.
As its proportion of total series resistance falls, its share of supply voltage/output p.d. decreases.
questions.modelAnswer: Output p.d. falls because lower-element thermistor resistance falls.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 1
questions.prompt: For N₂(g)+3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), write the Kp expression in partial pressures.
questions.modelAnswer: Kp=(pNH₃)²/((pN₂)(pH₂)³).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 2
questions.prompt: At equilibrium N₂, H₂ and NH₃ have partial pressures 100, 300 and 200 kPa respectively for N₂+3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Calculate Kp in kPa⁻².

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 3
questions.prompt: Explain why adding an inert gas at constant volume does not shift a gas-phase equilibrium expressed through Kp.
markPoints: Partial pressures of reacting gases remain unchanged at fixed volume and temperature.
The reaction quotient is therefore unchanged.
questions.modelAnswer: Partial pressures of reacting gases remain unchanged at fixed volume and temperature. The reaction quotient is therefore unchanged.
answerVariants: Partial pressures stay the same so Qp does not change
All reacting gas partial pressures remain constant so the equilibrium remains unchanged
No shift because partial pressures do not change at fixed volume
The partial pressures are unchanged and therefore Kp equilibrium position stays the same

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 4
questions.prompt: For 2SO₂(g)+O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0. State the effect of increasing temperature on Kp and explain.
markPoints: The endothermic reverse direction becomes more favoured.
questions.modelAnswer: Kp decreases as temperature increases. The endothermic reverse direction becomes more favoured.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 5
questions.prompt: Explain what it means for a monoprotic acid to be weak in water.
markPoints: Only a small proportion of acid molecules ionise; there is a reversible equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer: Only a small proportion of acid molecules ionise; there is a reversible equilibrium.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 6
questions.prompt: For a weak acid HA with concentration 0.100 mol dm⁻³ and [H⁺]=0.00100 mol dm⁻³, estimate Ka assuming little dissociation.
questions.modelAnswer: Ka≈[H⁺]²/[HA]. Ka≈1.00×10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 7
questions.prompt: A weak monoprotic acid has Ka=4.0×10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ and concentration 0.250 mol dm⁻³. Calculate its approximate pH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 8
questions.prompt: Explain why a weak acid and a strong acid of equal initial concentration have different pH values.
markPoints: The strong acid is essentially fully ionised.
The weak acid is only partly ionised, giving a lower hydrogen-ion concentration and higher pH.
questions.modelAnswer: The strong acid is essentially fully ionised. The weak acid is only partly ionised, giving a lower hydrogen-ion concentration and higher pH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 9
questions.prompt: Give the organic product of reacting ethanoic acid with propan-1-ol using an acid catalyst.
questions.modelAnswer: Propyl ethanoate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 10
questions.prompt: Write a word equation for acid-catalysed hydrolysis of methyl propanoate with water.
markPoints: Methyl propanoate + water ⇌ propanoic acid + methanol.
questions.modelAnswer: Methyl propanoate + water ⇌ propanoic acid + methanol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 11
questions.prompt: Describe how reflux differs from simple distillation during preparation of an ester.
markPoints: Reflux condenses vapours and returns them to the reaction vessel.
Distillation removes and collects volatile products as they vaporise.
questions.modelAnswer: Reflux condenses vapours and returns them to the reaction vessel. Distillation removes and collects volatile products as they vaporise.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Practice 12
questions.prompt: In an esterification reaction, explain one reason why the isolated product yield may be less than 100%.
markPoints: Esterification is reversible and may not go to completion.
Product may also be lost during transfer or purification.
questions.modelAnswer: Esterification is reversible and may not go to completion. Product may also be lost during transfer or purification.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Practice 13
questions.prompt: A current of 3.0 A flows perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.40 T. A straight conductor length 0.20 m is in the field. Find the force.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Practice 14
questions.prompt: State what is meant by magnetic flux density using the force on a current-carrying conductor.
markPoints: Magnetic flux density is force per unit current per unit length for a conductor perpendicular to the magnetic field.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnetic flux density is force per unit current per unit length for a conductor perpendicular to the magnetic field.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Practice 15
questions.prompt: A wire carries current towards you out of the page while the magnetic field is to the right. State the direction of the force using Fleming's left-hand rule.
questions.modelAnswer: The force acts upwards.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Practice 16
questions.prompt: Explain why a charged particle moving parallel to a uniform magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.
markPoints: Magnetic force is F=BQv sin θ.
For θ=0, sin θ=0 so magnetic force is zero.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnetic force is F=BQv sin θ. For θ=0, sin θ=0 so magnetic force is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Practice 17
questions.prompt: A ball is projected horizontally at 8.0 m s⁻¹ from a height of 20 m. Neglect air resistance, use g=9.81 m s⁻². Calculate time to reach the ground.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Practice 18
questions.prompt: A ball travels horizontally at 8.0 m s⁻¹ for 2.0 s without air resistance. Find its horizontal displacement.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Practice 19
questions.prompt: Explain why the horizontal velocity of a projectile is constant when air resistance is negligible.
markPoints: No resultant horizontal force acts on the projectile.
questions.modelAnswer: No resultant horizontal force acts on the projectile. Therefore horizontal acceleration is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Practice 20
questions.prompt: At the highest point of an angled projectile's trajectory (ignoring air resistance), describe its vertical velocity and acceleration.
markPoints: The vertical velocity is instantaneously zero.
The vertical acceleration remains g downwards.
questions.modelAnswer: The vertical velocity is instantaneously zero. The vertical acceleration remains g downwards.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Measurements 1
questions.prompt: A measured wire diameter is 0.42 mm ± 0.01 mm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the diameter.
markPoints: Percentage uncertainty is absolute uncertainty divided by reading multiplied by 100.
questions.modelAnswer: Percentage uncertainty is absolute uncertainty divided by reading multiplied by 100. 100×0.01/0.42 = 2.38%, approximately 2.4%.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Measurements 2
questions.prompt: Two students obtain mean values close to the true g, but one set is much more widely spread. Distinguish accuracy from precision using this example.
markPoints: Accuracy describes closeness of a result to the accepted value.
Precision describes the spread or repeatability of readings.
A set can be accurate on average yet have low precision.
questions.modelAnswer: Accuracy describes closeness of a result to the accepted value. Precision describes the spread or repeatability of readings. A set can be accurate on average yet have low precision.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Measurements 3
questions.prompt: A balance reads 0.03 g before an empty container is placed on it. The container then reads 15.82 g. Explain the zero error and give the corrected container mass.
markPoints: The balance has a positive zero offset of 0.03 g.
questions.modelAnswer: The balance has a positive zero offset of 0.03 g. Corrected mass = 15.82 − 0.03 = 15.79 g.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Measurements 4
questions.prompt: A rectangle has length 14.0 ± 0.1 cm and width 8.0 ± 0.1 cm. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in its area.
markPoints: Add fractional uncertainties in length and width for a product.
questions.modelAnswer: Add fractional uncertainties in length and width for a product. 100×(0.1/14.0+0.1/8.0) ≈ 1.96%.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Kinematics 5
questions.prompt: A bicycle speeds up uniformly from 4.0 to 16.0 m s⁻¹ over 6.0 s. Determine its acceleration and displacement.
markPoints: Average speed = 10 m s⁻¹, so displacement = 60 m.
questions.modelAnswer: Acceleration (16−4)/6 = 2.0 m s⁻². Average speed = 10 m s⁻¹, so displacement = 60 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Kinematics 6
questions.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest. Ignore air resistance. Calculate the time taken to fall 19.6 m using g = 9.81 m s⁻².
questions.modelAnswer: Apply s=ut+½at² with u=0. t=√(2×19.6/9.81) ≈ 2.00 s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Kinematics 7
questions.prompt: An object is thrown vertically upwards at 14.7 m s⁻¹. Find its maximum height above release, assuming g=9.81 m s⁻².
markPoints: Use v²=u²+2as with final v=0 and a=−9.81.
questions.modelAnswer: Use v²=u²+2as with final v=0 and a=−9.81. Height = 14.7²/(2×9.81) ≈ 11.0 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Kinematics 8
questions.prompt: A ball leaves a level table horizontally at 3.0 m s⁻¹ and lands 0.80 s later. Ignore air resistance. Find the horizontal range and vertical distance fallen.
questions.modelAnswer: Horizontal range = 3.0×0.80 = 2.4 m. Vertical distance = ½×9.81×0.80² ≈ 3.14 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Equilibrium 9
questions.prompt: A book rests on a desk without accelerating. State the two forces on it and explain their balance.
markPoints: Weight acts vertically down; the normal contact force acts vertically up.
They have equal magnitude so the resultant force is zero.
questions.modelAnswer: Weight acts vertically down; the normal contact force acts vertically up. They have equal magnitude so the resultant force is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Equilibrium 10
questions.prompt: An object is moving at a constant non-zero velocity. Must the resultant force be zero? Explain with Newton's first law.
markPoints: Yes; constant velocity means zero acceleration.
According to Newton's first law the resultant external force is zero.
questions.modelAnswer: Yes; constant velocity means zero acceleration. According to Newton's first law the resultant external force is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Equilibrium 11
questions.prompt: Two opposite horizontal forces of 32 N and 18 N act on a trolley. What extra horizontal force is needed for equilibrium? Give its direction.
markPoints: The existing net force is 14 N towards the 32 N force.
A 14 N force in the opposite direction is required.
questions.modelAnswer: The existing net force is 14 N towards the 32 N force. A 14 N force in the opposite direction is required.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Equilibrium 12
questions.prompt: A 60 N lamp is supported symmetrically by two cables, each at 30° to the horizontal. Calculate the tension in each cable.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertical components balance: 2T sin30° = 60. T=60 N in each cable.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Resolving vectors 13
questions.prompt: A force of 45 N acts 35° above the horizontal. Calculate its horizontal component.
markPoints: Horizontal is adjacent to the given angle.
questions.modelAnswer: Horizontal is adjacent to the given angle. Fₓ = 45 cos35° ≈ 36.9 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Resolving vectors 14
questions.prompt: The same 45 N force acts 35° above horizontal. Calculate its vertical component, explaining whether to use sine or cosine.
markPoints: Vertical component lies opposite the marked angle, so use sine.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertical component lies opposite the marked angle, so use sine. Fᵧ =45 sin35° ≈ 25.8 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Forces on a slope 15
questions.prompt: A 12 kg block is on a 25° slope. Calculate the component of its weight acting down the slope (g=9.81 m s⁻²).
markPoints: The downslope component is mg sinθ.
questions.modelAnswer: The downslope component is mg sinθ. 12×9.81×sin25° ≈ 49.7 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Forces on a slope 16
questions.prompt: A 12 kg block is on a 25° slope. With no other perpendicular forces, calculate the normal reaction.
markPoints: The perpendicular component is mg cosθ.
questions.modelAnswer: The perpendicular component is mg cosθ. R=12×9.81×cos25° ≈ 107 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Forces on a slope 17
questions.prompt: A block slides down a rough incline at constant speed. Explain the force balance parallel to the slope.
markPoints: The downslope component of weight is mg sinθ.
Constant velocity means friction balances mg sinθ.
questions.modelAnswer: The downslope component of weight is mg sinθ. Friction acts up the slope. Constant velocity means friction balances mg sinθ.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Couples 18
questions.prompt: Give three defining features of a pair of forces which form a couple.
markPoints: The two forces are equal in magnitude.
Their lines of action are parallel but separated.
questions.modelAnswer: The two forces are equal in magnitude. They act in opposite directions. Their lines of action are parallel but separated.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Couples 19
questions.prompt: A spanner is turned by two equal and opposite tangential forces of 12 N whose lines of action are 0.30 m apart. Calculate the moment of the couple.
markPoints: Moment of couple equals one force times perpendicular separation.
questions.modelAnswer: Moment of couple equals one force times perpendicular separation. 12×0.30 = 3.6 N m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Couples 20
questions.prompt: Why does a couple rotate an object without giving it a resultant translational force?
markPoints: The equal and opposite forces cancel as vectors.
Their separated lines of action nevertheless produce a turning moment.
questions.modelAnswer: The equal and opposite forces cancel as vectors. Their separated lines of action nevertheless produce a turning moment.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Moments 21
questions.prompt: A 25 N downward force is applied 0.40 m from a pivot, perpendicular to a lever. Calculate the turning moment.
questions.modelAnswer: Moment = force × perpendicular distance. 25×0.40=10 N m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Moments 22
questions.prompt: A uniform 2.0 m beam is balanced at its centre. A 6 N force acts downwards 0.50 m left of the pivot. At what distance on the right must a 3 N downward force act?
questions.modelAnswer: Clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance. 6×0.50=3×d, giving d=1.0 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Newton's laws 23
questions.prompt: A 5.0 kg object experiences forces 32 N right and 7 N left. Calculate acceleration and state its direction.
markPoints: F=ma gives a=25/5.0=5.0 m s⁻² right.
questions.modelAnswer: Resultant force = 25 N to right. F=ma gives a=25/5.0=5.0 m s⁻² right.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Newton's laws 24
questions.prompt: A swimmer pushes water backwards and accelerates forwards. Explain why these are Newton's third-law forces and why they do not cancel.
markPoints: The swimmer pushes on the water, and the water pushes forwards on the swimmer.
The interaction forces are equal and opposite and act on different bodies.
They do not cancel because they act on different objects.
questions.modelAnswer: The swimmer pushes on the water, and the water pushes forwards on the swimmer. The interaction forces are equal and opposite and act on different bodies. They do not cancel because they act on different objects.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Internal resistance 25
questions.prompt: A battery has emf 12.0 V and internal resistance 0.60 Ω. Find its terminal p.d. when delivering a current of 2.5 A.
questions.modelAnswer: Lost volts = Ir =2.5×0.60=1.50 V. Terminal p.d. = 12.0−1.50=10.5 V.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Internal resistance 26
questions.prompt: The terminal p.d. of a cell is 1.42 V at 0.40 A and 1.30 V at 1.00 A. Assuming V=ε−Ir, calculate internal resistance.
markPoints: The magnitude of the voltage-current graph gradient equals r.
questions.modelAnswer: The magnitude of the voltage-current graph gradient equals r. r=(1.42−1.30)/(1.00−0.40)=0.20 Ω.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Internal resistance 27
questions.prompt: Explain why terminal p.d. falls as current rises in a cell with a fixed emf.
markPoints: There is internal resistance in the cell.
The lost volts Ir grow as current grows.
questions.modelAnswer: There is internal resistance in the cell. The lost volts Ir grow as current grows. Terminal p.d. V=ε−Ir consequently decreases.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Photoelectric effect 28
questions.prompt: Increasing the intensity of red light fails to emit photoelectrons from a metal. What does this tell you about its frequency and why is intensity ineffective?
markPoints: Light frequency is below the metal's threshold frequency.
Each photon has energy hf below the work function.
More low-energy photons do not provide enough energy to emit electrons.
questions.modelAnswer: Light frequency is below the metal's threshold frequency. Each photon has energy hf below the work function. More low-energy photons do not provide enough energy to emit electrons.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Photoelectric effect 29
questions.prompt: A metal has work function 2.8 eV. It is illuminated with photons of 4.0 eV. Find the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy conservation gives Kmax=hf−work function. Kmax=4.0−2.8=1.2 eV.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Materials 30
questions.prompt: A metal wire has length 2.0 m, cross-sectional area 1.5×10⁻⁶ m² and extends 1.2 mm under a 90 N load. Calculate Young modulus.
questions.modelAnswer: Stress=90/(1.5×10⁻⁶)=6.0×10⁷ Pa. Strain=0.0012/2.0=6.0×10⁻⁴. E=stress/strain=1.0×10¹¹ Pa.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Materials 31
questions.prompt: Describe how a force–extension graph differs for an ideal spring and a ductile metal past its limit of proportionality.
markPoints: Ideal spring: straight line through the origin over the elastic range.
Ductile metal: gradient changes after limit of proportionality; plastic deformation may follow.
questions.modelAnswer: Ideal spring: straight line through the origin over the elastic range. Ductile metal: gradient changes after limit of proportionality; plastic deformation may follow.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Materials 32
questions.prompt: A spring's force increases uniformly from zero to 80 N as it extends 0.25 m. Calculate elastic energy stored.
markPoints: Energy equals area under force–extension graph.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy equals area under force–extension graph. E=½×80×0.25=10 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP6 EMF/internal resistance 33
questions.prompt: In an emf/internal-resistance experiment, a variable external resistance is adjusted and terminal p.d. V plotted against current I. Explain how emf and internal resistance are obtained.
markPoints: Equation V=ε−Ir predicts a straight line.
The V-axis intercept is emf ε.
The negative gradient has magnitude internal resistance r.
questions.modelAnswer: Equation V=ε−Ir predicts a straight line. The V-axis intercept is emf ε. The negative gradient has magnitude internal resistance r.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP6 EMF/internal resistance 34
questions.prompt: State why an ammeter should be in series and a voltmeter across the cell terminals when investigating internal resistance.
markPoints: The ammeter measures the current flowing through the external circuit.
The voltmeter measures terminal potential difference in parallel with the cell.
questions.modelAnswer: The ammeter measures the current flowing through the external circuit. The voltmeter measures terminal potential difference in parallel with the cell.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP6 EMF/internal resistance 35
questions.prompt: A student measures (I,V) = (0.50 A, 1.40 V) and (1.50 A, 1.10 V). Determine emf and internal resistance assuming V=ε−Ir.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP6 EMF/internal resistance 36
questions.prompt: Give two ways to reduce systematic effects during a measurement of emf and internal resistance.
markPoints: Keep the cell from warming significantly by switching off between readings.
Use high-resistance voltmeter to minimise current drawn by voltmeter.
Take a wide range of current measurements and plot a best-fit line.
questions.modelAnswer: Keep the cell from warming significantly by switching off between readings. Use high-resistance voltmeter to minimise current drawn by voltmeter. Take a wide range of current measurements and plot a best-fit line.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Kw 1
questions.prompt: At 25 °C, Kw = 1.00×10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. Calculate the pH of a solution in which [OH⁻] = 2.0×10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.
questions.modelAnswer: Use [H⁺]=Kw/[OH⁻]=5.0×10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³. pH=−log₁₀(5.0×10⁻¹⁰)≈9.30.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Kw 2
questions.prompt: At 25 °C, a solution has pH 3.60. Calculate [OH⁻] using Kw = 1.00×10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Kw 3
questions.prompt: Explain why pure water can have a pH below 7 when heated but still be neutral.
markPoints: Water ionisation is endothermic, so Kw increases as temperature rises.
Both ion concentrations increase equally; the water remains neutral.
questions.modelAnswer: Water ionisation is endothermic, so Kw increases as temperature rises. Neutrality means [H⁺]=[OH⁻], not necessarily pH 7. Both ion concentrations increase equally; the water remains neutral.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Kw 4
questions.prompt: Write the ionic product expression for water and explain why Kw changes with temperature.
markPoints: The equilibrium H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻ has a temperature-dependent equilibrium constant.
questions.modelAnswer: Kw=[H⁺][OH⁻] (concentrations at equilibrium). The equilibrium H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻ has a temperature-dependent equilibrium constant.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP3 Rates 1
questions.prompt: In a sodium thiosulfate and acid disappearing-cross experiment, the cross vanishes after 80 s in one run and 50 s in another. Estimate the relative rate increase.
questions.modelAnswer: Rate proxy is 1/t. (1/50)/(1/80)=80/50=1.6, a 60% increase.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP3 Rates 2
questions.prompt: Describe two variables to control when comparing disappearing-cross times at different thiosulfate concentrations.
markPoints: Keep temperature constant because it changes reaction rate.
Keep the total liquid volume, acid volume/concentration or optical path length constant.
Use the same viewing position and cross where possible.
questions.modelAnswer: Keep temperature constant because it changes reaction rate. Keep the total liquid volume, acid volume/concentration or optical path length constant. Use the same viewing position and cross where possible.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP3 Rates 3
questions.prompt: Why is disappearance of a cross only a proxy for rate rather than a direct measurement of instantaneous reaction rate?
markPoints: The cross becomes invisible when a roughly fixed amount of sulfur precipitate obscures it.
1/t estimates mean rate to a visual endpoint rather than an instantaneous gradient.
The endpoint can be subjective between observers.
questions.modelAnswer: The cross becomes invisible when a roughly fixed amount of sulfur precipitate obscures it. 1/t estimates mean rate to a visual endpoint rather than an instantaneous gradient. The endpoint can be subjective between observers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP3 Rates 4
questions.prompt: A graph of 1/t against sodium thiosulfate concentration is approximately a straight line through the origin at constant temperature. Explain its implication.
markPoints: Rate proxy is approximately proportional to thiosulfate concentration over the tested range.
The result is consistent with first-order dependence in thiosulfate for those conditions, but 1/t is an approximation.
questions.modelAnswer: Rate proxy is approximately proportional to thiosulfate concentration over the tested range. The result is consistent with first-order dependence in thiosulfate for those conditions, but 1/t is an approximation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP5 Distillation 1
questions.prompt: Explain why simple distillation can separate a volatile product from a mixture containing less volatile substances.
markPoints: The more volatile liquid enters the vapour phase more readily.
Vapour cools and condenses in the condenser.
The condensate is collected separately from higher-boiling material.
questions.modelAnswer: The more volatile liquid enters the vapour phase more readily. Vapour cools and condenses in the condenser. The condensate is collected separately from higher-boiling material.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP5 Distillation 2
questions.prompt: Where is a thermometer bulb positioned in a distillation apparatus, and what does it measure?
markPoints: It should be level with the entrance to the condenser/vapour outlet.
It records the temperature of vapour passing to the condenser, not the flask liquid directly.
questions.modelAnswer: It should be level with the entrance to the condenser/vapour outlet. It records the temperature of vapour passing to the condenser, not the flask liquid directly.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP5 Distillation 3
questions.prompt: Distinguish reflux from distillation when heating an organic reaction mixture.
markPoints: During reflux, vapour condenses and returns to the flask, limiting loss of volatile reactants.
During distillation, the condensed vapour is collected in a separate vessel.
questions.modelAnswer: During reflux, vapour condenses and returns to the flask, limiting loss of volatile reactants. During distillation, the condensed vapour is collected in a separate vessel.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP5 Distillation 4
questions.prompt: Why is a narrow, nearly constant boiling-temperature interval evidence of purity, rather than proof of absolute purity?
markPoints: A pure liquid at fixed pressure has a characteristic boiling point.
Mixtures often boil over a broader range.
Some impurities or azeotropes can give narrow boiling ranges; a single measurement is not conclusive.
questions.modelAnswer: A pure liquid at fixed pressure has a characteristic boiling point. Mixtures often boil over a broader range. Some impurities or azeotropes can give narrow boiling ranges; a single measurement is not conclusive.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP6 Organic tests 1
questions.prompt: An unknown compound forms an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH but no silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Identify a likely functional group and justify.
markPoints: 2,4-DNPH indicates a carbonyl group (aldehyde or ketone).
Negative Tollens' test favours a ketone rather than an aldehyde.
questions.modelAnswer: 2,4-DNPH indicates a carbonyl group (aldehyde or ketone). Negative Tollens' test favours a ketone rather than an aldehyde.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP6 Organic tests 2
questions.prompt: An organic sample decolourises bromine water at room temperature. State the likely functional group and explain the test's limitation.
markPoints: A carbon–carbon double bond in an alkene can react by electrophilic addition and decolourise bromine water.
Other reducing or bromine-reactive substances can also give a result; one test alone is not definitive.
questions.modelAnswer: A carbon–carbon double bond in an alkene can react by electrophilic addition and decolourise bromine water. Other reducing or bromine-reactive substances can also give a result; one test alone is not definitive.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP6 Organic tests 3
questions.prompt: A substance reacts with aqueous sodium carbonate to produce an effervescence. Give the likely acid functional group and gas produced.
markPoints: A carboxylic acid group –COOH reacts with carbonate.
Carbon dioxide gas causes the effervescence.
questions.modelAnswer: A carboxylic acid group –COOH reacts with carbonate. Carbon dioxide gas causes the effervescence.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: RP6 Organic tests 4
questions.prompt: Give a chemical test that distinguishes propanal from propanone, including the observations.
markPoints: Propanal gives a silver mirror (or brick-red precipitate with Fehling's); propanone does not.
questions.modelAnswer: Use Tollens' reagent (or Fehling's solution). Propanal gives a silver mirror (or brick-red precipitate with Fehling's); propanone does not.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Periodicity 1
questions.prompt: Explain the general decrease in atomic radius from sodium to chlorine across Period 3.
markPoints: Proton number/nuclear charge increases across the period.
Electrons are added to the same principal shell, so shielding changes relatively little.
The increased effective nuclear attraction draws the outer shell closer.
questions.modelAnswer: Proton number/nuclear charge increases across the period. Electrons are added to the same principal shell, so shielding changes relatively little. The increased effective nuclear attraction draws the outer shell closer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Periodicity 2
questions.prompt: Explain why aluminium's first ionisation energy is lower than magnesium's despite a larger nuclear charge.
markPoints: The electron removed from Al is a 3p electron rather than a 3s electron in Mg.
The 3p electron is higher in energy/more shielded and is easier to remove.
questions.modelAnswer: The electron removed from Al is a 3p electron rather than a 3s electron in Mg. The 3p electron is higher in energy/more shielded and is easier to remove.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Periodicity 3
questions.prompt: Explain why the first ionisation energy of sulfur is lower than phosphorus.
markPoints: Both have outer electrons in 3p orbitals.
Sulfur has one paired 3p orbital whereas phosphorus has three singly occupied 3p orbitals.
Repulsion between paired electrons makes removal easier in sulfur.
questions.modelAnswer: Both have outer electrons in 3p orbitals. Sulfur has one paired 3p orbital whereas phosphorus has three singly occupied 3p orbitals. Repulsion between paired electrons makes removal easier in sulfur.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Periodicity 4
questions.prompt: Predict the acidic or basic nature of Na₂O and SO₃ and give one suitable reaction equation for either.
markPoints: Na₂O is basic while SO₃ is acidic.
For example Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, or SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.
questions.modelAnswer: Na₂O is basic while SO₃ is acidic. For example Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, or SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Carboxylic acids 1
questions.prompt: Ethanoic acid reacts with aqueous sodium carbonate. Write the balanced equation and name the gas.
questions.modelAnswer: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂. The gas is carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Carboxylic acids 2
questions.prompt: Compare the acid strength of ethanoic acid and ethanol in water using stability of their conjugate bases.
markPoints: Ethanoate ion is resonance-stabilised with negative charge delocalised over two oxygen atoms.
Ethoxide does not have comparable delocalisation.
Ethanoic acid loses H⁺ more readily than ethanol.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethanoate ion is resonance-stabilised with negative charge delocalised over two oxygen atoms. Ethoxide does not have comparable delocalisation. Ethanoic acid loses H⁺ more readily than ethanol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Carboxylic acids 3
questions.prompt: Write the reversible reaction of propanoic acid with ethanol. Name the ester produced.
questions.modelAnswer: CH₃CH₂COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O. The ester is ethyl propanoate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Carboxylic acids 4
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between ester formation from an acyl chloride and from a carboxylic acid.
markPoints: Acyl chloride plus alcohol forms an ester and HCl, normally readily without equilibrium conditions.
Carboxylic acid plus alcohol is a reversible acid-catalysed esterification producing water.
questions.modelAnswer: Acyl chloride plus alcohol forms an ester and HCl, normally readily without equilibrium conditions. Carboxylic acid plus alcohol is a reversible acid-catalysed esterification producing water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Organic chemistry 1
questions.prompt: Distinguish a structural isomer from a stereoisomer.
markPoints: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity.
Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangements.
questions.modelAnswer: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity. Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangements.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Organic chemistry 2
questions.prompt: What happens to the bonding electrons in homolytic versus heterolytic fission?
markPoints: Homolytic fission gives one bonding electron to each atom and forms radicals.
Heterolytic fission gives both electrons to one atom and forms ions.
questions.modelAnswer: Homolytic fission gives one bonding electron to each atom and forms radicals. Heterolytic fission gives both electrons to one atom and forms ions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Organic chemistry 3
questions.prompt: Define a homologous series and state two characteristic features.
markPoints: Members have the same functional group and general formula.
They have similar chemical properties and show gradual changes in physical properties.
questions.modelAnswer: Members have the same functional group and general formula. Successive members differ by CH₂. They have similar chemical properties and show gradual changes in physical properties.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Organic chemistry 4
questions.prompt: Explain the terms electrophile and nucleophile by referring to an electron pair.
markPoints: An electrophile accepts an electron pair.
A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a covalent bond.
questions.modelAnswer: An electrophile accepts an electron pair. A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a covalent bond.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Group 2 1
questions.prompt: Explain the change in reactivity of Group 2 metals with water down the group.
markPoints: The outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded.
They are removed more easily, so the metals oxidise more readily.
questions.modelAnswer: Reactivity generally increases down Group 2. The outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded. They are removed more easily, so the metals oxidise more readily.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Group 2 2
questions.prompt: Describe the trend in solubility of Group 2 hydroxides down the group and one practical consequence.
markPoints: Group 2 hydroxide solubility generally increases down the group.
For example Ba(OH)₂ is more soluble than Mg(OH)₂.
questions.modelAnswer: Group 2 hydroxide solubility generally increases down the group. For example Ba(OH)₂ is more soluble than Mg(OH)₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Group 2 3
questions.prompt: Explain why a solution of barium chloride gives a white precipitate with sulfate ions.
markPoints: Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ form insoluble BaSO₄.
Net ionic equation: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s).
questions.modelAnswer: Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ form insoluble BaSO₄. Net ionic equation: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Group 7 1
questions.prompt: Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution. State the observation and explain electron transfer.
markPoints: Cl₂ oxidises Br⁻ to Br₂; chlorine gains electrons and is reduced.
questions.modelAnswer: An orange/brown bromine solution appears. Cl₂ oxidises Br⁻ to Br₂; chlorine gains electrons and is reduced. Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Group 7 2
questions.prompt: Explain why iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine.
markPoints: Down the group the atoms are larger, with more shielding.
The ability to attract and gain an electron decreases.
Chlorine is more readily reduced and is the stronger oxidising agent.
questions.modelAnswer: Down the group the atoms are larger, with more shielding. The ability to attract and gain an electron decreases. Chlorine is more readily reduced and is the stronger oxidising agent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Group 7 3
questions.prompt: A solution gives a cream precipitate with acidified silver nitrate. Identify the likely halide and state its formula.
markPoints: Bromide ions are indicated by the cream precipitate.
questions.modelAnswer: Bromide ions are indicated by the cream precipitate. Precipitate is silver bromide, AgBr(s).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Alkenes 1
questions.prompt: Give the essential condition for E/Z isomerism about a C=C bond.
markPoints: Each carbon atom in the double bond must have two different substituents.
Restricted rotation about the C=C makes alternative spatial arrangements isolable.
questions.modelAnswer: Each carbon atom in the double bond must have two different substituents. Restricted rotation about the C=C makes alternative spatial arrangements isolable.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Alkenes 2
questions.prompt: Outline the mechanism of adding HBr to propene, explaining the major organic product.
markPoints: The π bond attacks H⁺ from polarised HBr, forming the more stable secondary carbocation.
questions.modelAnswer: The π bond attacks H⁺ from polarised HBr, forming the more stable secondary carbocation. Br⁻ then attacks that carbocation. Major product is 2-bromopropane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Alkenes 3
questions.prompt: A hydrocarbon with formula C₄H₈ decolourises bromine water. Give one suitable displayed/structural isomer and explain why the colour disappears.
markPoints: A valid alkene is but-1-ene, but-2-ene or 2-methylpropene.
Bromine adds across the C=C double bond and its colour disappears.
questions.modelAnswer: A valid alkene is but-1-ene, but-2-ene or 2-methylpropene. Bromine adds across the C=C double bond and its colour disappears.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Aromatic chemistry 1
questions.prompt: Explain why benzene is more stable than the hypothetical cyclohexatriene with three isolated double bonds.
markPoints: Each carbon has a p orbital; six π electrons are delocalised around the ring.
Delocalisation lowers the energy of the molecule.
Benzene has equal C–C bond lengths and a lower enthalpy of hydrogenation than expected.
questions.modelAnswer: Each carbon has a p orbital; six π electrons are delocalised around the ring. Delocalisation lowers the energy of the molecule. Benzene has equal C–C bond lengths and a lower enthalpy of hydrogenation than expected.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Aromatic chemistry 2
questions.prompt: State the electrophile in nitration of benzene and explain its formation from nitric and sulfuric acids without giving a laboratory procedure.
markPoints: Electrophile is the nitronium ion NO₂⁺.
Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid and water is lost to generate NO₂⁺.
questions.modelAnswer: Electrophile is the nitronium ion NO₂⁺. Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid and water is lost to generate NO₂⁺.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Aromatic chemistry 3
questions.prompt: Describe the electrophilic substitution mechanism in nitration of benzene, including restoration of aromaticity.
markPoints: Benzene π electrons attack NO₂⁺ to form a positively charged intermediate.
A proton is lost to reform the delocalised π system.
questions.modelAnswer: Benzene π electrons attack NO₂⁺ to form a positively charged intermediate. A proton is lost to reform the delocalised π system. Product is nitrobenzene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Aromatic chemistry 4
questions.prompt: Why does benzene usually undergo electrophilic substitution instead of addition?
markPoints: Addition would destroy its delocalised aromatic π system.
Substitution restores/preserves aromatic stability after replacement of a hydrogen.
questions.modelAnswer: Addition would destroy its delocalised aromatic π system. Substitution restores/preserves aromatic stability after replacement of a hydrogen.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Transition metals 1
questions.prompt: Give two characteristic features of transition-metal chemistry linked to partially filled d orbitals.
markPoints: Transition elements form one or more stable ions with an incomplete d subshell.
They often form coloured complex ions and catalytic species.
questions.modelAnswer: Transition elements form one or more stable ions with an incomplete d subshell. Variable oxidation states are common. They often form coloured complex ions and catalytic species.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Transition metals 2
questions.prompt: Explain how the colour of many transition-metal complexes arises.
markPoints: Ligands split the metal ion's d orbitals into different energy levels.
Electrons absorb specific visible wavelengths and undergo d–d transitions.
questions.modelAnswer: Ligands split the metal ion's d orbitals into different energy levels. Electrons absorb specific visible wavelengths and undergo d–d transitions. The complementary colour is observed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Transition metals 3
questions.prompt: Define a ligand and coordination number, using [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ as an example.
markPoints: Ligand is an ion or molecule donating a lone pair to the central metal ion.
Coordination number counts coordinate bonds; [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ has coordination number 6.
questions.modelAnswer: Ligand is an ion or molecule donating a lone pair to the central metal ion. Coordination number counts coordinate bonds; [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ has coordination number 6.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Transition metals 4
questions.prompt: Explain why a catalyst that cycles between two oxidation states can speed up a redox reaction.
markPoints: It offers an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy.
The catalyst changes oxidation state in intermediate steps but is regenerated overall.
questions.modelAnswer: It offers an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy. The catalyst changes oxidation state in intermediate steps but is regenerated overall.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Amines 1
questions.prompt: Explain why methylamine behaves as a Brønsted–Lowry base in water.
markPoints: The nitrogen lone pair can accept a proton.
questions.modelAnswer: The nitrogen lone pair can accept a proton. CH₃NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃NH₃⁺ + OH⁻.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Amines 2
questions.prompt: Compare the basicity of phenylamine and methylamine, referring to the nitrogen lone pair.
markPoints: In phenylamine the lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring and less available to accept H⁺.
In methylamine the alkyl group donates electron density, making the lone pair more available.
questions.modelAnswer: In phenylamine the lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring and less available to accept H⁺. In methylamine the alkyl group donates electron density, making the lone pair more available. Methylamine is the stronger base.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Amines 3
questions.prompt: Name CH₃CH₂NH₂ and write an equation for its reaction with aqueous HCl.
questions.modelAnswer: The compound is ethanamine (ethylamine). CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Amines 4
questions.prompt: Classify (CH₃)₂NH as a primary, secondary or tertiary amine and justify.
markPoints: The nitrogen is bonded to two carbon-containing groups.
questions.modelAnswer: It is a secondary amine. The nitrogen is bonded to two carbon-containing groups.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Algebra 1
questions.prompt: Simplify (x²−9)/(x²−3x), giving every excluded value of x.
markPoints: Original expression excludes x=0 and x=3.
questions.modelAnswer: Factor as (x−3)(x+3)/[x(x−3)]. Simplified expression is (x+3)/x. Original expression excludes x=0 and x=3.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Algebra 2
questions.prompt: Complete the square for 2x²−8x+11 and give its minimum value.
questions.modelAnswer: Factor 2 from the quadratic/linear terms. 2x²−8x+11=2(x−2)²+3. Minimum value is 3 at x=2.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Algebra 3
questions.prompt: Factorise x³−4x²−x+4 completely over the real numbers.
markPoints: Group terms or identify a root using the factor theorem.
questions.modelAnswer: Group terms or identify a root using the factor theorem. Obtain (x−4)(x²−1). Complete as (x−4)(x−1)(x+1).

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Algebra 4
questions.prompt: Solve the equation |2x−3|=5, giving both values of x.
questions.modelAnswer: Split into 2x−3=5 and 2x−3=−5. Obtain x=4 and x=−1.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Differential equations 1
questions.prompt: Given dy/dx=3x² and y(1)=5, determine y explicitly in terms of x.
questions.modelAnswer: Integrate to obtain y=x³+C. Apply y(1)=5 to give C=4. So y=x³+4.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Differential equations 2
questions.prompt: Solve dy/dx=2xy given y(0)=3. Give y as a function of x.
questions.modelAnswer: Separate as (1/y)dy=2x dx. Integrate to ln|y|=x²+C. With y(0)=3, y=3e^(x²).

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Differential equations 3
questions.prompt: A quantity follows dN/dt=kN with N(0)=20 and N(2)=40. Determine k.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Differential equations 4
questions.prompt: Solve dy/dx=4/y with y(0)=2, assuming y remains positive.
questions.modelAnswer: Separate to y dy=4 dx. Integrate to y²/2=4x+C. Apply y(0)=2 to obtain y=√(8x+4).

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Statistics 1
questions.prompt: For observations 2, 3, 5 and 10, calculate the arithmetic mean.
questions.modelAnswer: Add to obtain 20. Divide by four: mean =5.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Statistics 2
questions.prompt: Two events A and B are independent, with P(A)=0.4 and P(B)=0.3. Find P(A∩B).
questions.modelAnswer: Independent events satisfy P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). 0.4×0.3=0.12.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Statistics 3
questions.prompt: Let X~B(5,0.2). Calculate P(X=2) to four significant figures.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Statistics 4
questions.prompt: If X is normally distributed with mean 100 and standard deviation 15, find P(X>115) to three significant figures.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Mechanics 1
questions.prompt: An object has initial velocity 2 m s⁻¹ and constant acceleration 3 m s⁻². Find its velocity after 4 s.
questions.modelAnswer: Use v=u+at. v=2+3×4=14 m s⁻¹.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Mechanics 2
questions.prompt: A 5 kg trolley is pushed with a horizontal 60 N force while friction is 10 N opposite motion. Find its acceleration.
questions.modelAnswer: Resultant force =60−10=50 N. a=F/m=50/5=10 m s⁻².

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Mechanics 3
questions.prompt: A 3 kg mass rests on a horizontal table and is connected over a smooth pulley to a hanging 2 kg mass. Neglect friction. Find acceleration.
markPoints: Net driving force is hanging weight 2g.
questions.modelAnswer: Net driving force is hanging weight 2g. Total accelerating mass is 5 kg. a=2×9.81/5≈3.92 m s⁻².

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Mechanics 4
questions.prompt: A box has normal contact force 50 N and coefficient of limiting friction 0.40. Determine maximum static friction.
questions.modelAnswer: Use Fmax=μR. Fmax=0.40×50=20 N.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Proof 1
questions.prompt: Disprove the claim 'Every odd integer greater than 1 is prime' using a counterexample.
markPoints: Give an odd composite integer such as 9.
Explain 9=3×3, so it is not prime.
questions.modelAnswer: Give an odd composite integer such as 9. Explain 9=3×3, so it is not prime.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Proof 2
questions.prompt: Explain how a proof by contradiction establishes that a conclusion must hold.
markPoints: Assume the opposite of the required conclusion.
Deduce a logical impossibility or contradiction with a known premise.
Therefore the initial assumption is false, so the conclusion must be true.
questions.modelAnswer: Assume the opposite of the required conclusion. Deduce a logical impossibility or contradiction with a known premise. Therefore the initial assumption is false, so the conclusion must be true.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Logs 1
questions.prompt: Find x if log₂(x)=5.
questions.modelAnswer: Convert to x=2⁵. Hence x=32.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Logs 2
questions.prompt: Simplify ln(3x)−ln(x), where x>0.
questions.modelAnswer: Use ln a−ln b=ln(a/b). Result ln3.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Logs 3
questions.prompt: Solve ln(x−1)=2 and state the domain restriction.
questions.modelAnswer: Exponentiate: x−1=e². x=1+e²≈8.39. Valid because x>1.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Numerical methods 1
questions.prompt: Show that the continuous function f(x)=x³−x−1 has a root in (1,2).
markPoints: Opposite signs and continuity imply a root in (1,2).
questions.modelAnswer: f(1)=1−1−1=−1. f(2)=8−2−1=5. Opposite signs and continuity imply a root in (1,2).

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Numerical methods 2
questions.prompt: Use one Newton–Raphson iteration for f(x)=x²−2, starting at x₁=1.5. Give x₂ to four decimal places.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Transformations 1
questions.prompt: Describe the transformation of y=f(x) to y=f(x−3)+2.
questions.modelAnswer: Translation 3 units right (inside x−3). Translation 2 units upwards (outside +2).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP1 Stationary waves 1
markPoints: Three loops correspond to three half-wavelengths.
questions.modelAnswer: Three loops correspond to three half-wavelengths. 3λ/2=0.75 m, so λ=0.50 m.
questions.prompt: In a string vibration experiment, a stretched segment of length 0.75 m contains three loops. Calculate the wavelength.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP1 Stationary waves 2
markPoints: A single loop is λ/2=0.25 m.
questions.modelAnswer: λ=v/f=60/120=0.50 m. A single loop is λ/2=0.25 m.
questions.prompt: A stretched string vibrates at 120 Hz, with wave speed 60 m s⁻¹. Find the length of a single-loop stationary wave.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: RP1 Stationary waves 3
markPoints: Several node spacings make the measured length larger.
This reduces percentage uncertainty in the estimated wavelength.
questions.modelAnswer: Several node spacings make the measured length larger. This reduces percentage uncertainty in the estimated wavelength.
questions.prompt: Why is the distance between adjacent nodes measured over several loops rather than one in a stationary-wave practical?
