The crate travels 5.00 m. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate (a) the component of weight down the slope, (b) friction on the crate, and (c) work done by the applied force over the 5.00 m. Explain why friction acts down the slope.
markPoints: Weight component down slope = 75.0 × 9.81 × sin18° ≈ 227 N.
Applied-force component up the slope = 320 cos12° ≈ 313 N.
Constant velocity means the resultant force parallel to the slope is zero.
Work by applied force = Fs cos12° = 320 × 5.00 × cos12° ≈ 1565 J.
Friction opposes the relative motion of the sliding crate up the surface.
questions.modelAnswer: Weight component down slope = 75.0 × 9.81 × sin18° ≈ 227 N. Applied-force component up the slope = 320 cos12° ≈ 313 N. Constant velocity means the resultant force parallel to the slope is zero. Friction = 313 − 227 ≈ 85.6 N down the slope. Work by applied force = Fs cos12° = 320 × 5.00 × cos12° ≈ 1565 J. Friction opposes the relative motion of the sliding crate up the surface.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A 12.0 V cell has internal resistance 1.00 Ω. It supplies two resistors of 6.00 Ω and 3.00 Ω connected in parallel. Calculate the total current supplied by the cell, its terminal potential difference, the current through each parallel branch, and the energy dissipated in the internal resistance during 90.0 s. Assume all resistances are constant.
markPoints: Branch currents: I₆Ω = 8.00/6.00 = 1.33 A and I₃Ω = 8.00/3.00 = 2.67 A.
Power wasted in cell = I²r = 16.0 W.
Energy lost in 90.0 s = I²rt = 1440 J.
questions.modelAnswer: Parallel external resistance: (1/6.00 + 1/3.00)⁻¹ = 2.00 Ω. Total circuit resistance is 2.00 + 1.00 = 3.00 Ω. Total current = ε/Rtotal = 12.0/3.00 = 4.00 A. Terminal p.d. = ε − Ir = 12.0 − 4.00 × 1.00 = 8.00 V. Branch currents: I₆Ω = 8.00/6.00 = 1.33 A and I₃Ω = 8.00/3.00 = 2.67 A. Power wasted in cell = I²r = 16.0 W. Energy lost in 90.0 s = I²rt = 1440 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: In a Young double-slit experiment, the distance across ten adjacent fringe spacings is (26.4 ± 0.5) mm. The slit separation is (0.320 ± 0.010) mm and the screen distance is (1.80 ± 0.02) m. Find the wavelength in nm, estimate its percentage uncertainty by adding percentage uncertainties, and state why measuring ten spacings is preferable to measuring one. Treat the quoted uncertainties as absolute.
markPoints: Use λ = ws/D with consistent SI units.
Ten fringes give a larger measurement distance, reducing the percentage uncertainty of reading a single fringe spacing.
questions.modelAnswer: One fringe spacing = 26.4/10 = 2.64 mm. Use λ = ws/D with consistent SI units. λ = 0.00264 × 0.000320 / 1.80 = 4.69 × 10⁻⁷ m = 469 nm. Percentage uncertainty from fringe measurement = 0.5/26.4 × 100 ≈ 1.89%. Add percentage uncertainties: 1.89% + 0.010/0.320 × 100 + 0.02/1.80 × 100 ≈ 6.13%. Ten fringes give a larger measurement distance, reducing the percentage uncertainty of reading a single fringe spacing.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A 0.250 kg mass is attached to an ideal horizontal spring with spring constant 40.0 N m⁻¹. The mass oscillates with amplitude 0.0600 m. Calculate (a) its angular frequency, (b) period, (c) maximum speed, (d) total oscillation energy and (e) speed when displacement is +0.0300 m. State any assumption used.
markPoints: Maximum speed vmax = Aω ≈ 0.759 m s⁻¹.
At x = +0.0300 m, speed ≈ 0.657 m s⁻¹.
Assumes ideal undamped SHM with negligible friction and massless spring.
questions.modelAnswer: Angular frequency ω = √(k/m) = √(40.0/0.250) ≈ 12.65 rad s⁻¹. Period T = 2π/ω ≈ 0.497 s. Maximum speed vmax = Aω ≈ 0.759 m s⁻¹. Total energy E = ½kA² = 0.0720 J. Use v² = ω²(A² − x²). At x = +0.0300 m, speed ≈ 0.657 m s⁻¹. Assumes ideal undamped SHM with negligible friction and massless spring.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: Two parallel metal plates are separated by 8.00 mm with a uniform potential difference of 400 V. An electron is released from rest at the negative plate and travels towards the positive plate. Assume no collisions and neglect edge effects. Given electron charge magnitude 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, calculate field strength, force magnitude, acceleration, kinetic energy gained and final speed. Explain the direction of the force relative to the field.
markPoints: Electric field magnitude E = V/d = 400/0.00800 = 5.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.
Kinetic energy gain is eV = 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.
Using ½mv² = eV gives v ≈ 1.19 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
The electron is negatively charged, so force is opposite electric-field direction.
Uniform field and negligible collisions and edge effects are assumed.
questions.modelAnswer: Electric field magnitude E = V/d = 400/0.00800 = 5.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Force magnitude F = eE = 8.00 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. Acceleration a = F/m ≈ 8.78 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻². Kinetic energy gain is eV = 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. Using ½mv² = eV gives v ≈ 1.19 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. The electron is negatively charged, so force is opposite electric-field direction. Uniform field and negligible collisions and edge effects are assumed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A cylinder contains 0.0200 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K and volume 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³. First it is compressed isothermally to 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³. It is then heated at constant volume to 350 K. Given R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, calculate the pressure at all three stages and explain how each change follows from the gas laws. State two assumptions of the ideal-gas model.
markPoints: An ideal gas has negligible molecular volume compared with its container.
Its particles exert no intermolecular forces except during collisions (which are elastic).
questions.modelAnswer: Initially p₁=nRT/V₁=99,720 Pa ≈ 99.7 kPa. Isothermal compression gives p₁V₁=p₂V₂. After compression p₂ ≈ 166,200 Pa ≈ 166 kPa. At constant volume p₂/T₂=p₃/T₃. After heating p₃ = 166,200 × 350/300 ≈ 193,900 Pa. An ideal gas has negligible molecular volume compared with its container. Its particles exert no intermolecular forces except during collisions (which are elastic).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A 0.300 kg trolley moves at 4.00 m s⁻¹ and collides with a stationary 0.500 kg trolley. The two trolleys stick together. Calculate their common velocity, the total kinetic energy before and after, and the kinetic energy lost. Explain why this collision can conserve momentum but not kinetic energy, assuming no significant external impulse.
markPoints: Common velocity v = 1.50 m s⁻¹ in initial direction.
Momentum is conserved because external impulse is negligible.
Kinetic energy transforms to deformation, heat, sound or internal energy in the inelastic collision.
questions.modelAnswer: Conservation of momentum: (0.300 × 4.00) + (0.500 × 0) = (0.800)v. Common velocity v = 1.50 m s⁻¹ in initial direction. Initial kinetic energy = ½ × 0.300 × 4.00² = 2.40 J. Final kinetic energy = ½ × 0.800 × 1.50² = 0.900 J. Kinetic energy lost = 2.40 − 0.900 = 1.50 J. Momentum is conserved because external impulse is negligible. Kinetic energy transforms to deformation, heat, sound or internal energy in the inelastic collision.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A straight wire 0.300 m long carries current 3.00 A in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.450 T. The wire is at 30.0° to the magnetic field. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic force. If the wire moves 0.0800 m parallel to this force, determine the work done by the force. Explain what happens to the magnetic force if the wire is aligned parallel to the field.
markPoints: Force on a current-carrying wire is F=BIL sinθ.
The angle between wire/current direction and field is θ = 30.0°.
If wire is aligned parallel to B, θ=0 and the force is zero.
The magnetic force acts perpendicular to both field and current direction.
questions.modelAnswer: Force on a current-carrying wire is F=BIL sinθ. The angle between wire/current direction and field is θ = 30.0°. F = 0.450 × 3.00 × 0.300 × sin30° = 0.2025 N. Mechanical work W = F × 0.0800 = 0.0162 J. If wire is aligned parallel to B, θ=0 and the force is zero. The magnetic force acts perpendicular to both field and current direction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: An impure 0.850 g sample of calcium carbonate is added to 40.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ HCl. Once the carbonate has reacted, the remaining acid needs 18.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol dm⁻³ NaOH for complete neutralisation. Assume only CaCO₃ reacts with HCl, all excess acid is titrated, and Mᵣ(CaCO₃)=100.1. Calculate the percentage by mass of CaCO₃ in the original sample. State why HCl and NaOH react in a 1:1 mole ratio.
markPoints: The acid consumed by CaCO₃ is 0.0200 − 0.00720 = 0.01280 mol.
Reaction CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O gives 1:2 carbonate:acid ratio.
Neutralisation H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O requires one mole of NaOH per mole of HCl.
questions.modelAnswer: Initial n(HCl) = 0.0400 × 0.500 = 0.0200 mol. Remaining HCl = n(NaOH) = 0.0180 × 0.400 = 0.00720 mol. The acid consumed by CaCO₃ is 0.0200 − 0.00720 = 0.01280 mol. Reaction CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O gives 1:2 carbonate:acid ratio. n(CaCO₃)=0.01280/2=0.00640 mol. Mass pure CaCO₃ = 0.00640 × 100.1 = 0.64064 g. Percentage purity = 0.64064/0.850 × 100 ≈ 75.4%. Neutralisation H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O requires one mole of NaOH per mole of HCl.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: For a reaction, rate constant k is 0.0120 s⁻¹ at 300 K and 0.0500 s⁻¹ at 320 K. Use the two-temperature Arrhenius equation ln(k₂/k₁) = (Eₐ/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂) and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to calculate Eₐ in kJ mol⁻¹. Explain why k normally increases with temperature and why activation energy must be expressed with suitable units.
markPoints: At higher temperature a larger fraction of collisions have energy at least Eₐ.
R has units J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so Eₐ calculated this way is in J mol⁻¹ before conversion.
questions.modelAnswer: Take the ratio k₂/k₁ = 0.0500/0.0120 ≈ 4.167. Natural log of ratio ≈ 1.427. Compute 1/300 − 1/320 = 2.0833 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. Rearrange Eₐ = R ln(k₂/k₁)/(1/T₁−1/T₂). Eₐ ≈ 56,925 J mol⁻¹ = 56.9 kJ mol⁻¹. At higher temperature a larger fraction of collisions have energy at least Eₐ. R has units J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so Eₐ calculated this way is in J mol⁻¹ before conversion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ aqueous monoprotic acid HA has pH 3.00 at 25 °C. Calculate [H⁺], [A⁻], [HA] at equilibrium and Kₐ without making the approximation that the acid concentration is unchanged. Decide whether that approximation would nevertheless be reasonable here, using a percentage dissociation calculation. Assume water's contribution to [H⁺] is negligible.
markPoints: For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, [A⁻] = [H⁺] = 0.00100 mol dm⁻³.
Because dissociation is only 2%, treating [HA]≈0.0500 is a reasonable approximation.
questions.modelAnswer: [H⁺] = 10⁻³⋅⁰⁰ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, [A⁻] = [H⁺] = 0.00100 mol dm⁻³. Undissociated [HA] = 0.0500 − 0.00100 = 0.0490 mol dm⁻³. Kₐ = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. Kₐ = (0.00100)²/0.0490 = 2.04 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Fraction dissociated = 0.00100/0.0500 × 100 = 2.00%. Because dissociation is only 2%, treating [HA]≈0.0500 is a reasonable approximation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: At equilibrium at a fixed temperature, the reaction N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) has a total pressure of 200 kPa. The mixture contains 60.0% NO₂ and 40.0% N₂O₄ by mole fraction. Calculate both partial pressures and the numerical Kₚ with appropriate units. Predict and explain the direction of equilibrium shift when the volume is decreased at constant temperature.
markPoints: Decreasing volume raises pressure, favouring the side with fewer moles of gas.
Equilibrium shifts towards N₂O₄, the single-molecule side.
Kₚ remains constant at fixed temperature even though equilibrium partial pressures change.
questions.modelAnswer: Partial pressure of NO₂ = 0.600 × 200 = 120 kPa. Partial pressure of N₂O₄ = 0.400 × 200 = 80.0 kPa. Kₚ = (pNO₂)²/pN₂O₄. Kₚ=120²/80.0=180 kPa. Decreasing volume raises pressure, favouring the side with fewer moles of gas. Equilibrium shifts towards N₂O₄, the single-molecule side. Kₚ remains constant at fixed temperature even though equilibrium partial pressures change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: Benzoyl chloride, C₆H₅COCl, reacts with ethanol to produce an ester. Name and write the structural formula of the ester, give a balanced overall equation, outline the nucleophilic addition–elimination mechanism, and explain why the reaction is generally more rapid than esterification of the corresponding carboxylic acid with ethanol.
markPoints: Balanced equation: C₆H₅COCl + CH₃CH₂OH → C₆H₅COOCH₂CH₃ + HCl.
The lone pair on ethanol oxygen attacks the electrophilic acyl carbon.
C=O π bonding shifts to oxygen, creating a tetrahedral intermediate.
The carbonyl re-forms and chloride leaves (addition–elimination).
Loss of a proton gives the neutral ester product.
Acyl chlorides are more reactive electrophiles and do not depend on the slow acid-catalysed reversible esterification equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer: Product is ethyl benzoate, C₆H₅COOCH₂CH₃. Balanced equation: C₆H₅COCl + CH₃CH₂OH → C₆H₅COOCH₂CH₃ + HCl. The lone pair on ethanol oxygen attacks the electrophilic acyl carbon. C=O π bonding shifts to oxygen, creating a tetrahedral intermediate. The carbonyl re-forms and chloride leaves (addition–elimination). Loss of a proton gives the neutral ester product. Acyl chlorides are more reactive electrophiles and do not depend on the slow acid-catalysed reversible esterification equilibrium.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: For MgO(s), standard enthalpy of formation is −602 kJ mol⁻¹. Use these values (kJ mol⁻¹): Mg(s)→Mg(g) +150; Mg(g)→Mg⁺(g)+e⁻ +738; Mg⁺(g)→Mg²⁺(g)+e⁻ +1451; ½O₂(g)→O(g) +249; O(g)+e⁻→O⁻(g) −141; O⁻(g)+e⁻→O²⁻(g) +744. Determine the lattice enthalpy of formation of MgO(s) using a Born–Haber cycle and explain why the second electron affinity of oxygen is endothermic.
markPoints: Include atomisation/sublimation of Mg: +150 kJ mol⁻¹.
Include the two ionisation energies of Mg: +738 and +1451 kJ mol⁻¹.
Include atomisation of O: +249 kJ mol⁻¹.
Include the first and second electron affinities: −141 and +744 kJ mol⁻¹.
Sum gaseous-ion formation steps to +3191 kJ mol⁻¹.
Apply Hess's law: ΔfH° = sum of steps + ΔlattH°.
Lattice enthalpy of formation = −602 −3191 = −3793 kJ mol⁻¹.
The second electron is added to O⁻ and is repelled by an already negatively charged ion, so energy is required.
questions.modelAnswer: Include atomisation/sublimation of Mg: +150 kJ mol⁻¹. Include the two ionisation energies of Mg: +738 and +1451 kJ mol⁻¹. Include atomisation of O: +249 kJ mol⁻¹. Include the first and second electron affinities: −141 and +744 kJ mol⁻¹. Sum gaseous-ion formation steps to +3191 kJ mol⁻¹. Apply Hess's law: ΔfH° = sum of steps + ΔlattH°. Lattice enthalpy of formation = −602 −3191 = −3793 kJ mol⁻¹. The second electron is added to O⁻ and is repelled by an already negatively charged ion, so energy is required.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: Standard electrode potentials are E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V. Write the oxidation and reduction half-equations and the overall cell reaction. Calculate E°cell, identify the negative electrode, and explain why the standard potential alone cannot determine the reaction rate.
markPoints: Overall reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
Zinc is the negative electrode (anode) in the operating galvanic cell.
Positive E°cell indicates the overall cell reaction is thermodynamically favourable under standard conditions.
Reaction rate also depends on kinetics such as activation barriers, not just the potential difference.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidation at zinc: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. Reduction at copper: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). Overall reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. Zinc is the negative electrode (anode) in the operating galvanic cell. Positive E°cell indicates the overall cell reaction is thermodynamically favourable under standard conditions. Reaction rate also depends on kinetics such as activation barriers, not just the potential difference.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A compound has formula C₄H₈O₂ and three distinct proton NMR signals: δ 1.2 ppm (triplet, integration 3), δ 2.3 ppm (quartet, integration 2), and δ 3.7 ppm (singlet, integration 3). Suggest an ester structure, explain the splitting and integration of each signal, and justify why the total signal integration fits the molecular formula.
markPoints: The proposed ester is methyl propanoate CH₃CH₂COOCH₃.
Triplet at ~1.2 ppm integrates to 3H for CH₃ adjacent to CH₂.
Quartet at ~2.3 ppm integrates to 2H for CH₂ adjacent to CH₃ and carbonyl.
Singlet at ~3.7 ppm integrates to 3H for OCH₃ with no neighbouring proton on the adjacent oxygen.
The n+1 rule explains triplet from 2 neighbours and quartet from 3 neighbours.
The chemical shifts are consistent with alkyl group next to C=O and methoxy ester oxygen.
questions.modelAnswer: The proposed ester is methyl propanoate CH₃CH₂COOCH₃. Triplet at ~1.2 ppm integrates to 3H for CH₃ adjacent to CH₂. Quartet at ~2.3 ppm integrates to 2H for CH₂ adjacent to CH₃ and carbonyl. Singlet at ~3.7 ppm integrates to 3H for OCH₃ with no neighbouring proton on the adjacent oxygen. The n+1 rule explains triplet from 2 neighbours and quartet from 3 neighbours. Integrated protons total 3 + 2 + 3 = 8, matching C₄H₈O₂. The chemical shifts are consistent with alkyl group next to C=O and methoxy ester oxygen.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: Solve 2cos²θ − 3sinθ = 0 for 0 ≤ θ < 2π. Give all solutions exactly in radians, and explain why any extraneous algebraic value must be rejected.
markPoints: Reject sinθ = −2 because sine is restricted to [−1,1].
In interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π, solutions are θ=π/6 and θ=5π/6.
questions.modelAnswer: Use cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ. Rearrange to 2sin²θ + 3sinθ − 2 = 0. Factorise: (2sinθ − 1)(sinθ + 2) = 0. Algebra gives sinθ = 1/2 or sinθ = −2. Reject sinθ = −2 because sine is restricted to [−1,1]. In interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π, solutions are θ=π/6 and θ=5π/6.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: Let f(x) = (3x − 2)/(x + 1), defined for x > −1. Prove f is increasing, find its range, derive f⁻¹(x) and its domain, and calculate f⁻¹(1). Give exact answers where possible.
markPoints: Since f′(x)>0 for x>−1, f is strictly increasing.
For x>−1, f(x) tends to −∞ as x→−1+ and to 3 from below as x→∞.
questions.modelAnswer: Differentiate f to obtain f′(x)=5/(x+1)². Since f′(x)>0 for x>−1, f is strictly increasing. For x>−1, f(x) tends to −∞ as x→−1+ and to 3 from below as x→∞. Range is y<3. Rearrange y(x+1)=3x−2 to x=(y+2)/(3−y). Inverse f⁻¹(x)=(x+2)/(3−x), with domain x<3. f⁻¹(1)=3/2.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: The curves y=x² and y=2x+3 enclose a finite region. Find the x-coordinates of their intersections and calculate the exact area enclosed. Explain how you know which curve is above the other between intersections.
markPoints: At x=0, the line y=3 lies above parabola y=0.
Evaluate bounds to get 32/3 square units.
questions.modelAnswer: Set x²=2x+3 to obtain x²−2x−3=0. Factor (x−3)(x+1)=0 giving x=−1 and x=3. At x=0, the line y=3 lies above parabola y=0. Set area A=∫₋₁³[(2x+3)−x²] dx. Integrate to x²+3x−x³/3. Evaluate bounds to get 32/3 square units.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: An enclosure is built against an existing straight wall using 80 m of new fencing to form the other three sides of a rectangle. Let x be the length of each side perpendicular to the wall. Find the dimensions giving maximum area and prove it is a maximum.
markPoints: Set dA/dx=0 to get x=20 m.
Then y=40 m and maximum area A=20×40=800 m².
Second derivative d²A/dx²=−4<0 proves a maximum.
questions.modelAnswer: Fencing constraint is 2x+y=80, so y=80−2x. Area A=xy=80x−2x². Differentiate: dA/dx=80−4x. Set dA/dx=0 to get x=20 m. Then y=40 m and maximum area A=20×40=800 m². Second derivative d²A/dx²=−4<0 proves a maximum.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A 4.00 kg block lies on a horizontal rough surface and is connected over a smooth pulley by a light inextensible string to a hanging 3.00 kg mass. The constant friction force on the block is 5.00 N opposing motion. Assuming the system moves with the hanging mass descending, find the common acceleration and string tension. Use g=9.81 m s⁻². Explain any force balance you apply.
markPoints: Driving weight of hanging mass is 3.00g=29.43 N.
Friction opposes block motion, so net driving force on system is 29.43−5.00=24.43 N.
For hanging mass 3.00g−T=3.00a, giving the same tension.
questions.modelAnswer: Driving weight of hanging mass is 3.00g=29.43 N. Friction opposes block motion, so net driving force on system is 29.43−5.00=24.43 N. Combined accelerating mass is 4.00+3.00=7.00 kg. Acceleration a=24.43/7.00≈3.49 m s⁻². For the block, T−5.00=4.00a. Hence tension T≈18.96 N. For hanging mass 3.00g−T=3.00a, giving the same tension.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A factory uses machine A to make 60% of products and B to make 40%. Machine A produces defective items with probability 0.020, and B with probability 0.050. A product is selected at random and found defective. Find the overall probability of a defect and the conditional probability it came from machine B. Show how the two possible origins contribute.
questions.modelAnswer: P(A and defective)=0.60×0.020=0.0120. P(B and defective)=0.40×0.050=0.0200. P(defective)=0.0120+0.0200=0.0320. Apply conditional probability P(B|defect)=P(B∩defect)/P(defect). P(B|defect)=0.0200/0.0320=0.625.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A manufacturer claims the probability of a defective component is 0.20. A random sample of 20 components contains 9 defects. Test at the 5% significance level whether the defect probability has increased. Define hypotheses, the distribution under H₀, suitable critical region or p-value, and give a conclusion in context.
markPoints: The 5% upper-tail critical region is X≥8.
Observed X=9 is in the critical region.
Reject H₀; there is statistically significant evidence that defect probability increased.
The conclusion is about evidence, not proof that the probability definitely changed.
questions.modelAnswer: Set H₀:p=0.20 and H₁:p>0.20. Under H₀, X~Bin(20,0.20). Calculate P(X≥8)≈0.0321 and P(X≥7)≈0.0867. The 5% upper-tail critical region is X≥8. Observed X=9 is in the critical region. Reject H₀; there is statistically significant evidence that defect probability increased. The conclusion is about evidence, not proof that the probability definitely changed.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Extended application
questions.prompt: A geometric series begins with 81 and has common ratio 2/3. Calculate the sum to infinity and the sum of its first five terms. Find the smallest positive integer n for which the remainder after n terms is less than 10. Explain your inequality step.
markPoints: Remaining sum after n terms is 243(2/3)ⁿ.
Taking logarithms gives n>ln(10/243)/ln(2/3)≈7.87; inequality reverses when dividing by negative ln(2/3).
questions.modelAnswer: Since |r|<1, S∞=a/(1−r)=81/(1/3)=243. S₅=243[1−(2/3)⁵]=211. Remaining sum after n terms is 243(2/3)ⁿ. Require 243(2/3)ⁿ<10. Taking logarithms gives n>ln(10/243)/ln(2/3)≈7.87; inequality reverses when dividing by negative ln(2/3). Minimum integer n is 8.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 1
questions.prompt: Ethene reacts with HBr. On paper draw the full electrophilic addition mechanism with charges and every curly arrow. Alternatively describe where each arrow starts and ends. Identify the organic product.
markPoints: Show Hδ⁺–Brδ⁻ (or otherwise identify the polar H–Br bond).
First curly arrow goes from C=C π bond towards the H atom.
Second curly arrow goes from the H–Br bond to Br, giving Br⁻.
Show the CH₃CH₂⁺ carbocation intermediate with charge on carbon.
Arrow goes from a Br⁻ lone pair towards the carbocation carbon.
Final organic product is CH₃CH₂Br, bromoethane.
questions.modelAnswer: Show Hδ⁺–Brδ⁻ (or otherwise identify the polar H–Br bond). First curly arrow goes from C=C π bond towards the H atom. Second curly arrow goes from the H–Br bond to Br, giving Br⁻. Show the CH₃CH₂⁺ carbocation intermediate with charge on carbon. Arrow goes from a Br⁻ lone pair towards the carbocation carbon. Final organic product is CH₃CH₂Br, bromoethane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 2
questions.prompt: Propene reacts with HBr and produces two bromoalkane isomers. Draw or describe the two possible carbocations, give their classes and explain the major product using intermediate stability.
markPoints: One pathway forms a secondary carbocation: CH₃CH⁺CH₃.
The alternative pathway forms a primary carbocation: CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺.
The secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary one.
Attack by Br⁻ on the secondary carbocation gives 2-bromopropane.
Identify 2-bromopropane as major and 1-bromopropane as minor.
questions.modelAnswer: One pathway forms a secondary carbocation: CH₃CH⁺CH₃. The alternative pathway forms a primary carbocation: CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺. questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 3
questions.prompt: Bromine molecules are non-polar before they approach ethene. Explain their reaction and, on paper, draw a mechanism showing a polarised Br₂, the electron-pair movements and the product.
markPoints: C=C is an electron-rich π bond.
The π electrons induce a dipole in approaching Br₂; nearest Br becomes δ⁺.
Arrow from the C=C electron pair to the δ⁺ bromine atom.
Arrow from Br–Br bonding pair to the other bromine; Br⁻ forms.
A positively charged bromine-containing intermediate is attacked by Br⁻.
questions.modelAnswer: C=C is an electron-rich π bond. The π electrons induce a dipole in approaching Br₂; nearest Br becomes δ⁺. Arrow from the C=C electron pair to the δ⁺ bromine atom. Arrow from Br–Br bonding pair to the other bromine; Br⁻ forms. A positively charged bromine-containing intermediate is attacked by Br⁻. Product is CH₂BrCH₂Br, 1,2-dibromoethane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 4
questions.prompt: Ethene undergoes electrophilic addition with H₂SO₄. Draw or describe the arrow movements, intermediates and immediate organic product; then state how that product relates to ethanol.
markPoints: Ethene's C=C π electrons attack an H of H₂SO₄.
The O–H bonding pair goes to oxygen, giving HSO₄⁻.
The HSO₄⁻ oxygen donates a lone pair to the carbocation carbon.
The immediate product is CH₃CH₂OSO₃H (ethyl hydrogensulfate).
Hydrolysis of the alkyl hydrogensulfate yields ethanol.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethene's C=C π electrons attack an H of H₂SO₄. The O–H bonding pair goes to oxygen, giving HSO₄⁻. A CH₃CH₂⁺ carbocation forms. The HSO₄⁻ oxygen donates a lone pair to the carbocation carbon. The immediate product is CH₃CH₂OSO₃H (ethyl hydrogensulfate). Hydrolysis of the alkyl hydrogensulfate yields ethanol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 5
questions.prompt: A student draws OH⁻ attacking the Br atom in CH₃CH₂Br. Explain why this is wrong and draw or describe the corrected two-curly-arrow substitution mechanism, including product ions.
markPoints: C–Br is polar; its carbon is δ⁺.
OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile, donating a lone pair from O.
Arrow from O lone pair to the carbon attached to Br (not to Br).
Arrow from the C–Br bond to Br, forming Br⁻.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 6
questions.prompt: A halogenoalkane RBr reacts with ammonia to give a primary amine. Draw or describe the two stages with all charges, the initially formed organic ion and the subsequent proton transfer.
markPoints: NH₃ is a neutral nucleophile with a nitrogen lone pair.
Arrow from the N lone pair to the δ⁺ carbon bonded to Br.
Arrow from the C–Br bond to Br, which leaves as Br⁻.
The first organic intermediate is positively charged RNH₃⁺.
A second ammonia molecule accepts a proton from RNH₃⁺.
The organic product is RNH₂, a primary amine; NH₄⁺ is also formed.

The first organic intermediate is positively charged RNH₃⁺. A second ammonia molecule accepts a proton from RNH₃⁺. The organic product is RNH₂, a primary amine; NH₄⁺ is also formed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 7
questions.prompt: 2-Bromobutane can undergo elimination. Draw the concerted elimination mechanism on paper (or explain all three curly arrows). Identify the organic product types and why more than one alkene is possible.
markPoints: OH⁻ acts as a base and accepts a hydrogen from a β carbon.
First arrow: O lone pair of OH⁻ to a β hydrogen.
Second arrow: β C–H bond pair to the C–C bond, forming C=C.
Third arrow: C–Br bond electron pair to Br, giving Br⁻.
Products include an alkene, water and Br⁻.
Removing H from either adjacent carbon allows but-1-ene or but-2-ene; but-2-ene has E/Z forms.
questions.modelAnswer: OH⁻ acts as a base and accepts a hydrogen from a β carbon. First arrow: O lone pair of OH⁻ to a β hydrogen. Second arrow: β C–H bond pair to the C–C bond, forming C=C. Third arrow: C–Br bond electron pair to Br, giving Br⁻. Products include an alkene, water and Br⁻. Removing H from either adjacent carbon allows but-1-ene or but-2-ene; but-2-ene has E/Z forms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 8
questions.prompt: On paper set out the initiation, two propagation and two different termination equations for free-radical chlorination of methane. Explain why it is a chain reaction and why a mixture can form.
markPoints: Valid termination: Cl• + CH₃• → CH₃Cl (or equivalent).
Different valid termination: CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ (or Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂).
Radicals are regenerated in propagation, sustaining a chain.
Further substitution or alternative terminations give a product mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: Initiation under UV: Cl₂ → 2Cl•. Propagation 1: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•. Propagation 2: CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. Valid termination: Cl• + CH₃• → CH₃Cl (or equivalent). Different valid termination: CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ (or Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂). Radicals are regenerated in propagation, sustaining a chain. Further substitution or alternative terminations give a product mixture.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 9
questions.prompt: An exam question gives Cl• reacting with stratospheric ozone. Write the two radical steps and deduce the net equation. Explain why chlorine atoms are catalysts rather than reactants overall.
markPoints: Cl• is consumed in one step but regenerated in the next.
ClO• is an intermediate and cancels when equations are summed.
questions.modelAnswer: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂. ClO• + O₃ → Cl• + 2O₂. Cl• is consumed in one step but regenerated in the next. ClO• is an intermediate and cancels when equations are summed. Overall 2O₃ → 3O₂, with net ozone depletion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 10
questions.prompt: A generic alcohol undergoes acid-catalysed dehydration to give an alkene. Describe the electron and proton changes or draw a schematic curly-arrow mechanism; explain why the acid is a catalyst.
markPoints: Alcohol oxygen is protonated so –OH becomes –OH₂⁺.

The molecule loses water and a β hydrogen, creating C=C.
Deprotonation restores a neutral organic product.
The H⁺ catalyst is regenerated overall.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 11
questions.prompt: The monomer CH₂=CHCl forms a polymer. Draw the correctly bracketed repeating unit, with continuation bonds, and explain how you would recover the monomer from the unit.
markPoints: C=C becomes a single C–C bond in the backbone.
Cl remains a side group, not in the backbone.
Continuation bonds pass through each side of the brackets.
Monomer is reconstructed as CH₂=CHCl by restoring the C=C.

questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.prompt: For CH₃CH=CHCH₂OH: give the correct IUPAC name, explain whether E/Z isomerism is possible, and state a reliable method for determining E or Z from a displayed drawing.

Compare atomic numbers of directly attached atoms; move outward after ties.

questions.subject: Chemistry

Rising temperature suggests composition is changing towards higher-boiling components.
Collecting a narrow-boiling fraction gives some evidence of purity, not proof.

Returning product allows further oxidation instead of isolating it.
Distillation removes the more volatile product as it forms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 15

B is consistent with a carboxylic acid, producing CO₂.
C is consistent with an oxidisable alcohol (primary or secondary).
D contains an aldehyde group (carbonyl plus positive Tollens').
Some tests are not exclusive, so confirmation with complementary evidence is needed.

C is consistent with an oxidisable alcohol (primary or secondary). D contains an aldehyde group (carbonyl plus positive Tollens'). Some tests are not exclusive, so confirmation with complementary evidence is needed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 16
questions.prompt: Two unknown substances X and Y each give a positive 2,4-DNPH test. X also gives a Tollens' silver deposit; Y does not. Explain the conclusions, including what 2,4-DNPH alone cannot establish.

2,4-DNPH alone cannot distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone.
X is an aldehyde under these conditions because Tollens' is positive.

An independent test or spectrum can confirm identification.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Application 17
questions.prompt: A molecular sample has a strong IR absorption around 1700 cm⁻¹, no very broad O–H absorption from 2500–3300 cm⁻¹, and gives no Tollens' silver deposit. Explain the most likely carbonyl class and the limitations of each clue.

No broad acid O–H feature makes a carboxylic acid less likely.
Negative Tollens' result makes an ordinary aldehyde less likely.
A ketone is the most likely class under these conditions.
IR and chemical tests should be interpreted together; neither alone proves a unique structure.

questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.prompt: Three otherwise comparable halogenoalkanes show an observable silver-halide precipitate after 45 s (iodo), 90 s (bromo), and 180 s (chloro). Weaker C–X bond makes hydrolysis more rapid for otherwise comparable structures.

questions.subject: Chemistry

CH₂O₂ has exact neutral atomic mass 12.000000 + 2(1.007825) + 2(15.994915).

questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 1
questions.prompt: On paper, draw both three-dimensional enantiomers of butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, using solid and hashed wedges at the chiral carbon. Explain why your two drawings are enantiomers and predict how equal concentrations affect plane-polarised light.
markPoints: Carbon 2 is correctly identified as attached to CH₃, CH₂CH₃, H and OH.
Both drawings show a tetrahedral carbon with a clear three-dimensional wedge-and-dash representation.
All four attached groups retain the correct connectivity in each drawing.
The arrangement at the chiral carbon is inverted between the drawings, not merely rotated on the paper.
The two forms are non-superimposable mirror images.
Pure enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally in magnitude but in opposite directions under identical conditions.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon 2 is correctly identified as attached to CH₃, CH₂CH₃, H and OH. Both drawings show a tetrahedral carbon with a clear three-dimensional wedge-and-dash representation. All four attached groups retain the correct connectivity in each drawing. The arrangement at the chiral carbon is inverted between the drawings, not merely rotated on the paper. The two forms are non-superimposable mirror images. Pure enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally in magnitude but in opposite directions under identical conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 2
questions.prompt: A model glycerol triester contains one ethanoate, one propanoate and one butanoate residue, each attached to a different oxygen of glycerol. On paper, draw its complete condensed or displayed structure. Identify the linkages and predict the molecular products of complete hydrolysis. Do not give a laboratory method.
markPoints: The glycerol framework is correctly shown as CH₂–CH–CH₂ with an oxygen substituent on each carbon.
One oxygen is linked as –O–C(=O)–CH₃ (ethanoate residue).
A second oxygen is linked as –O–C(=O)–CH₂CH₃ (propanoate residue).
The third oxygen is linked as –O–C(=O)–CH₂CH₂CH₃ (butanoate residue).
All three –O–C(=O)– units are correctly recognised as ester links.
Complete acid hydrolysis yields one glycerol molecule and one molecule each of ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid.
questions.modelAnswer: The glycerol framework is correctly shown as CH₂–CH–CH₂ with an oxygen substituent on each carbon. One oxygen is linked as –O–C(=O)–CH₃ (ethanoate residue). A second oxygen is linked as –O–C(=O)–CH₂CH₃ (propanoate residue). The third oxygen is linked as –O–C(=O)–CH₂CH₂CH₃ (butanoate residue). All three –O–C(=O)– units are correctly recognised as ester links. Complete acid hydrolysis yields one glycerol molecule and one molecule each of ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 3
questions.prompt: A reference pure organic solid has a melting point of 122.4 °C. Sample A melts over 116.5–120.0 °C; sample B melts over 121.8–122.4 °C. Assess which sample is likely purer and what the data can and cannot prove.
markPoints: Sample B is more consistent with a pure sample than A.
Sample B has a narrower melting range of 0.6 °C.
Sample A has a broader melting range of 3.5 °C.
An impurity generally lowers and broadens the observed melting range of a solid.
The melting data alone do not establish the compound's identity or absolute purity conclusively.
questions.modelAnswer: Sample B is more consistent with a pure sample than A. Sample B has a narrower melting range of 0.6 °C. Sample A has a broader melting range of 3.5 °C. An impurity generally lowers and broadens the observed melting range of a solid. The melting data alone do not establish the compound's identity or absolute purity conclusively.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 4
questions.prompt: Hydrogenation of cyclohexene releases 120 kJ mol⁻¹. A hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with three isolated double bonds would therefore release three times this amount. The measured enthalpy change for hydrogenation of benzene is −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the theoretical value and the extra stabilisation of benzene, and explain what it implies about bonding and substitution.
markPoints: The theoretical value for three isolated C=C bonds is 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹.
The measured benzene hydrogenation enthalpy is less exothermic than −360 kJ mol⁻¹.
The stabilisation difference is 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹.
The π electrons in benzene are delocalised over the ring.
Delocalisation lowers the energy of benzene relative to the hypothetical three-isolated-bond structure.
Substitution is favoured over addition because it preserves the delocalised aromatic system.
questions.modelAnswer: The theoretical value for three isolated C=C bonds is 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹. The measured benzene hydrogenation enthalpy is less exothermic than −360 kJ mol⁻¹. The stabilisation difference is 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹. The π electrons in benzene are delocalised over the ring. Delocalisation lowers the energy of benzene relative to the hypothetical three-isolated-bond structure. Substitution is favoured over addition because it preserves the delocalised aromatic system.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 5
questions.prompt: On paper, draw a polyester repeating unit formed from propane-1,3-diol, HO–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–OH, and butanedioic acid, HOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOH. Use square brackets and continuation bonds. Explain the type of polymerisation and show the linkage that repeats.
markPoints: The three-carbon diol segment –O–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–O– appears in the repeat unit.
The diacid segment –C(=O)–CH₂–CH₂–C(=O)– appears in the repeat unit.
The oxygen of each alcohol-derived end connects to an acid-derived carbonyl carbon, forming ester links.
The repeating unit is correctly bracketed with bonds extending through the bracket edges.
This is condensation polymerisation with elimination of a small molecule such as water when bonds form.
questions.modelAnswer: The three-carbon diol segment –O–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–O– appears in the repeat unit. The diacid segment –C(=O)–CH₂–CH₂–C(=O)– appears in the repeat unit. The oxygen of each alcohol-derived end connects to an acid-derived carbonyl carbon, forming ester links. The repeating unit is correctly bracketed with bonds extending through the bracket edges. The link is identified as –C(=O)–O– (or –O–C(=O)–). This is condensation polymerisation with elimination of a small molecule such as water when bonds form.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 6
questions.prompt: A polyamide has the repeating unit [–NH–(CH₂)₄–NH–C(=O)–(CH₂)₂–C(=O)–]ₙ. On paper, draw the two monomers from which it was formed. Name the bond type between monomer fragments and explain the intermolecular attractions between typical polyamide chains.
markPoints: The repeating structure includes the amide linkage –C(=O)–NH–.
The carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds from N–H groups on adjacent polyamide chains.
Hydrogen bonding gives an intermolecular attraction between typical polyamide chains.
Amide linkages can undergo hydrolysis, unlike the all-carbon backbone of a typical polyalkene.
questions.modelAnswer: The diamine monomer is H₂N–(CH₂)₄–NH₂. The second monomer is HOOC–(CH₂)₂–COOH. The repeating structure includes the amide linkage –C(=O)–NH–. The carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds from N–H groups on adjacent polyamide chains. Hydrogen bonding gives an intermolecular attraction between typical polyamide chains. Amide linkages can undergo hydrolysis, unlike the all-carbon backbone of a typical polyalkene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 7
questions.prompt: For alanine, CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH, draw the predominant simple structural forms in acidic solution, as a zwitterion, and in alkaline solution. Label the overall charge on each. Use the protonation states rather than a practical method.
markPoints: The acidic form has overall charge +1.
The zwitterion has overall charge zero despite internal positive and negative charges.
The alkaline form has overall charge −1.
questions.modelAnswer: The acidic form is CH₃CH(NH₃⁺)COOH. The acidic form has overall charge +1. The zwitterion is CH₃CH(NH₃⁺)COO⁻. The zwitterion has overall charge zero despite internal positive and negative charges. The alkaline form is CH₃CH(NH₂)COO⁻. The alkaline form has overall charge −1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 8
questions.prompt: Draw the full condensed structural formula of the tripeptide Ala–Gly–Ser (alanine–glycine–serine) with a free N terminus on the alanine end. Use side chains –CH₃ for alanine, –H for glycine and –CH₂OH for serine. Label the peptide links, and describe what complete hydrolysis yields.
markPoints: The N terminus is H₂N–CH(CH₃)–C(=O)– for alanine.
Two correctly placed –C(=O)–NH– peptide linkages join the three residues.
The tripeptide has one free N terminus and one free carboxyl terminus.
Complete hydrolysis of the peptide bonds yields alanine, glycine and serine.
questions.modelAnswer: The N terminus is H₂N–CH(CH₃)–C(=O)– for alanine. The central glycine residue is –NH–CH₂–C(=O)–. The final serine residue is –NH–CH(CH₂OH)–COOH. Two correctly placed –C(=O)–NH– peptide linkages join the three residues. The tripeptide has one free N terminus and one free carboxyl terminus. Complete hydrolysis of the peptide bonds yields alanine, glycine and serine.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 9
questions.prompt: Three labelled drawings represent a protein: A shows just the ordered amino-acid sequence; B shows a section coiled into an α-helix with dotted links between backbone groups; C shows the whole chain folded, with a labelled sulfur–sulfur bridge between side chains. questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 10
questions.prompt: A fictional enzyme has an asymmetric active site with three binding regions. Enantiomer P positions all three matching groups towards these regions; its mirror image Q can align only two groups at once. Explain why the enzyme can discriminate between P and Q, and why this need not imply a difference in their molecular formulae.
markPoints: P and Q are enantiomers with the same molecular formula and connectivity.
They have different three-dimensional arrangements and are non-superimposable mirror images.
The enzyme's active site has a specific three-dimensional shape and binding-group arrangement.
P can position all three complementary groups for favourable binding.
Q cannot necessarily achieve the same three-point alignment, so it may bind more weakly or not react.
This is stereospecificity; it depends on spatial fit and interactions, not simply chemical composition.
questions.modelAnswer: P and Q are enantiomers with the same molecular formula and connectivity. They have different three-dimensional arrangements and are non-superimposable mirror images. The enzyme's active site has a specific three-dimensional shape and binding-group arrangement. P can position all three complementary groups for favourable binding. Q cannot necessarily achieve the same three-point alignment, so it may bind more weakly or not react. This is stereospecificity; it depends on spatial fit and interactions, not simply chemical composition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 11
questions.prompt: A compound has formula C₃H₆O₂. Its ¹³C NMR spectrum has three environments, with shifts near δ 20, 52 and 171 ppm. Its ¹H spectrum has just two singlets, each integrating to 3 H, near δ 2.1 and 3.7 ppm. Distinguish methyl ethanoate (CH₃COOCH₃) from propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH), using all the data.
markPoints: The molecular formula is consistent with either of the stated structural isomers.
Three ¹³C environments are consistent with the three non-equivalent carbon atoms in methyl ethanoate.
The carbon near δ 171 ppm is consistent with a carbonyl environment.
The two ¹H integrations of 3:3 show two distinct three-proton environments.
Two singlets fit methyl ethanoate's CH₃CO– and –OCH₃ groups, without neighbouring non-equivalent hydrogens on adjacent carbon atoms.
Propanoic acid would give a CH₃ triplet and CH₂ quartet in the simple first-order model, not two three-proton singlets.
The supported structure is methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃.
questions.modelAnswer: The molecular formula is consistent with either of the stated structural isomers. Three ¹³C environments are consistent with the three non-equivalent carbon atoms in methyl ethanoate. The carbon near δ 171 ppm is consistent with a carbonyl environment. The two ¹H integrations of 3:3 show two distinct three-proton environments. Two singlets fit methyl ethanoate's CH₃CO– and –OCH₃ groups, without neighbouring non-equivalent hydrogens on adjacent carbon atoms. Propanoic acid would give a CH₃ triplet and CH₂ quartet in the simple first-order model, not two three-proton singlets. The supported structure is methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 12
questions.subtopic: Interpret a complete TLC mixture and standards

The upper U spot has Rf = 6.0/8.0 = 0.75.
Under the same conditions, U's lower spot matches standard A.
Under the same conditions, U's upper spot matches standard C, with no spot matching B.
Matching Rf values are suggestive rather than conclusive proof of chemical identity; another solvent or analysis could provide confirmation.

Under the same conditions, U's lower spot matches standard A. Under the same conditions, U's upper spot matches standard C, with no spot matching B. Matching Rf values are suggestive rather than conclusive proof of chemical identity; another solvent or analysis could provide confirmation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 13
questions.prompt: A gas chromatogram recorded under fixed conditions has standards A, B and C with retention times 2.40, 5.20 and 7.90 minutes. An unknown has two peaks at 2.42 and 5.18 minutes. No peak close to C's 7.90-minute retention time is shown.
Identification by retention time must use comparable chromatographic conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 organic application 14
questions.subtopic: Recognise amine and ammonium structural classes
questions.prompt: On paper, draw the displayed or condensed formulae of methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine and the tetramethylammonium cation. Label each as primary, secondary, tertiary or quaternary. Explain how the nitrogen lone pair differs in the cation.
markPoints: CH₃NH₂ is a primary amine with one carbon-containing substituent on nitrogen.
(CH₃)₂NH is a secondary amine with two carbon-containing substituents.
(CH₃)₃N is a tertiary amine with three carbon-containing substituents.
(CH₃)₄N⁺ is a quaternary ammonium cation with four carbon-containing substituents.
The quaternary ammonium nitrogen has a formal positive charge.
The quaternary ammonium ion has no available nitrogen lone pair, unlike the neutral amines.

(CH₃)₃N is a tertiary amine with three carbon-containing substituents. (CH₃)₄N⁺ is a quaternary ammonium cation with four carbon-containing substituents. The quaternary ammonium nitrogen has a formal positive charge. The quaternary ammonium ion has no available nitrogen lone pair, unlike the neutral amines.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 mechanism/route 1

This is a theoretical drawing exercise; no reagent preparations or experimental conditions are required.
markPoints: The attacking arrow starts from the lone pair on H⁻ and ends at the electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
A second electron-pair arrow starts at the C=O π bond and ends on oxygen.
The first-stage tetrahedral intermediate is correctly drawn as R–CH₂–O⁻.
The intermediate oxygen bears the negative formal charge.
The protonation arrow starts at the alkoxide oxygen lone pair and ends at the supplied H⁺.
The final structure is R–CH₂–OH, a primary alcohol.
The student explains that the two hydrogen equivalents have been added across the original carbonyl group.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 mechanism/route 2
questions.subtopic: Ketone reduction: electron movement and equation
questions.prompt: A theoretical ketone R–C(=O)–R′ is reduced by the model nucleophile H⁻ and then protonated by H⁺. Draw the curved-arrow mechanism on paper and supply an overall structural equation using 2[H]. Explain how the alcohol class differs from reduction of a typical aldehyde.
markPoints: A curly arrow shows H⁻ electron-pair donation to the carbonyl carbon.
The C=O π electrons move to the oxygen atom.
The intermediate is R–C(H)(O⁻)–R′ with tetrahedral carbon.
The alkoxide oxygen is protonated to form R–CH(OH)–R′.
The overall equation is R–C(=O)–R′ + 2[H] → R–CH(OH)–R′.
The ketone yields a secondary alcohol when R and R′ are both carbon-containing groups.
A typical aldehyde gives a primary alcohol under the corresponding reduction.
questions.modelAnswer: A curly arrow shows H⁻ electron-pair donation to the carbonyl carbon. The C=O π electrons move to the oxygen atom. The intermediate is R–C(H)(O⁻)–R′ with tetrahedral carbon. questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 mechanism/route 4
questions.subtopic: Addition–elimination arrow logic using abstract groups
questions.prompt: A model acyl derivative R–C(=O)–LG is represented with an unspecified leaving group LG. A generic nitrogen lone-pair donor :NH₂R′ attacks. The C=O π electrons shift to oxygen during nucleophilic addition.
The intermediate has a tetrahedral carbonyl-derived carbon bearing O⁻, LG and the nitrogen substituent.

The C–LG bond electrons transfer to LG, so the leaving group departs.
A proton transfer gives the neutral framework R–C(=O)–NHR′.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 mechanism/route 5
questions.subtopic: Electrophilic aromatic substitution with supplied acyl electrophile

questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.subtopic: Nucleophilic substitution by a neutral nitrogen donor

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 mechanism/route 7
questions.subtopic: Repeated nitrogen substitution: structures and charges

The primary, secondary and tertiary labels count carbon-containing groups bonded directly to nitrogen.
