questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 mechanism/route 10
questions.subtopic: Four-step route percentage yield and waste
questions.prompt: A fictional paper synthesis A→B→C→D→E uses four conceptual transformations with individual percentage yields 80.0%, 75.0%, 90.0% and 60.0%. Calculate the total yield expressed as a fraction of the theoretical maximum, and find the mass of E if the maximum possible mass would be 40.0 g. Explain two reasons why chemists prefer shorter, high-atom-economy routes. This question does not involve planning a laboratory procedure.
markPoints: The first two percentages are represented as fractions 0.800 and 0.750.
All four fractional step yields are multiplied: 0.800 × 0.750 × 0.900 × 0.600.
The expected final mass is 40.0 × 0.324 = 12.96 g, approximately 13.0 g.
Additional steps tend to compound losses and can increase separation and energy requirements.
High atom economy puts a greater fraction of reactant atoms into the desired product and can reduce by-product waste.
questions.modelAnswer: The first two percentages are represented as fractions 0.800 and 0.750. All four fractional step yields are multiplied: 0.800 × 0.750 × 0.900 × 0.600. The overall yield fraction is 0.324. The overall percentage yield is 32.4%. The expected final mass is 40.0 × 0.324 = 12.96 g, approximately 13.0 g. Additional steps tend to compound losses and can increase separation and energy requirements. High atom economy puts a greater fraction of reactant atoms into the desired product and can reduce by-product waste.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 mechanism/route 11
questions.subtopic: Evaluate two routes to the same theoretical product
questions.prompt: Two abstract four-step routes to the SAME benign polymer precursor are shown only as mass balances. Route P has steps of 90%, 90%, 80%, 85% yield. Route Q has two steps at 75% yield each. No chemical identities or reaction conditions are supplied. Calculate each overall yield, compare them and explain why a route with fewer steps is not automatically safer unless hazards and atom economy are considered.
markPoints: Route P total fractional yield is 0.90 × 0.90 × 0.80 × 0.85.
Route Q total fractional yield is 0.75 × 0.75.
On the supplied yields, Q gives a slightly higher overall yield.
Step count alone does not establish hazard or environmental impact; solvent demand and material hazards matter.
Atom economy concerns the share of reactant atoms retained in the desired product, not percentage yield alone.
questions.modelAnswer: Route P total fractional yield is 0.90 × 0.90 × 0.80 × 0.85. Route P overall yield is 0.5508 = 55.08%. Route Q total fractional yield is 0.75 × 0.75. Route Q overall yield is 0.5625 = 56.25%. On the supplied yields, Q gives a slightly higher overall yield. Step count alone does not establish hazard or environmental impact; solvent demand and material hazards matter. Atom economy concerns the share of reactant atoms retained in the desired product, not percentage yield alone.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A2 mechanism/route 12
questions.subtopic: Check wrong curly arrows in addition–elimination
questions.prompt: A fictional student's paper mechanism for generic R–C(=O)–LG and :NH₂R′ shows: (i) an arrow from carbonyl oxygen to the nitrogen lone pair, (ii) an arrow from C=O towards oxygen during attack, (iii) elimination of LG while the carbonyl reforms. Identify which arrows are correctly oriented, repair the incorrect arrow, and explain how the formal charge on the tetrahedral intermediate arises. No real substances or preparation details are required.
markPoints: Arrow (i) is wrong: electron-pair donation must start at the nitrogen lone pair.
The corrected nucleophilic arrow points from nitrogen to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
Arrow (ii), from C=O π bonding electrons to oxygen, is correctly oriented.
After donation the nitrogen has four bonds and is formally positive (before proton transfer).
The intermediate oxygen has a negative charge from receiving the π-electron pair.
The elimination step reforms C=O and transfers C–LG bond electrons to the leaving group.
The mechanism is nucleophilic addition–elimination and produces a carbonyl-containing nitrogen derivative after proton transfer.
questions.modelAnswer: Arrow (i) is wrong: electron-pair donation must start at the nitrogen lone pair. The corrected nucleophilic arrow points from nitrogen to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon. Arrow (ii), from C=O π bonding electrons to oxygen, is correctly oriented. After donation the nitrogen has four bonds and is formally positive (before proton transfer). The intermediate oxygen has a negative charge from receiving the π-electron pair. The elimination step reforms C=O and transfers C–LG bond electrons to the leaving group. The mechanism is nucleophilic addition–elimination and produces a carbonyl-containing nitrogen derivative after proton transfer.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 mock application 1
questions.prompt: A velocity–time graph has three straight segments: (i) from t=0 to 4.0 s, velocity is +6.0 m s⁻¹; (ii) from 4.0 to 7.0 s it falls linearly from +6.0 to −3.0 m s⁻¹; (iii) from 7.0 to 9.0 s it remains at −3.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate net displacement and total distance; identify the direction of motion from 7.0 to 9.0 s.
markPoints: On the second interval, v=0 at t=6.0 s.
Second-interval positive area is ½ × 2.0 × 6.0 = +6.0 m.
Second-interval negative area is ½ × 1.0 × 3.0 = −1.5 m.
Total distance is 24 + 6 + 1.5 + 6 = 37.5 m; last interval is negative-direction travel.
questions.modelAnswer: First interval displacement is +6.0 × 4.0 = +24 m. On the second interval, v=0 at t=6.0 s. Second-interval positive area is ½ × 2.0 × 6.0 = +6.0 m. Second-interval negative area is ½ × 1.0 × 3.0 = −1.5 m. Third interval displacement is −3.0 × 2.0 = −6.0 m. Total displacement is 24 + 6 − 1.5 − 6 = +22.5 m. Total distance is 24 + 6 + 1.5 + 6 = 37.5 m; last interval is negative-direction travel.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 mock application 2
questions.prompt: On an unfamiliar curved displacement–time graph, a tangent at t=3.0 s passes through two clearly read points (1.0 s, 4.0 m) and (5.0 s, 20.0 m). Determine the instantaneous velocity at t=3.0 s, state its direction and explain why using a tangent is appropriate rather than finding the gradient of the whole curve.
markPoints: A tangent to the displacement–time curve is used at the specified instant.
Change in displacement along tangent is 20.0 − 4.0 = 16.0 m.
Positive gradient indicates motion in the positive direction.
The tangent gives instantaneous velocity whereas a chord over a time interval gives average velocity.
questions.modelAnswer: A tangent to the displacement–time curve is used at the specified instant. Change in displacement along tangent is 20.0 − 4.0 = 16.0 m. Change in time is 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0 s. Tangent gradient = 16.0/4.0 = +4.0 m s⁻¹. Positive gradient indicates motion in the positive direction. The tangent gives instantaneous velocity whereas a chord over a time interval gives average velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 mock application 3
questions.subtopic: Horizontal projectile launched from a raised platform
questions.prompt: A ball leaves a raised platform horizontally at 16.0 m s⁻¹ and lands 45.0 m below its launch point. Ignore air resistance, and use g=9.81 m s⁻². Calculate time of flight, horizontal distance, vertical component of impact velocity and magnitude of impact velocity. Explain why horizontal and vertical components share the same flight time.
markPoints: Horizontal acceleration is zero; horizontal velocity stays 16.0 m s⁻¹.
Vertically, displacement −45.0 m = ½(−9.81)t², giving t = √(90.0/9.81) = 3.03 s.
Horizontal and vertical motion occur simultaneously, so the same elapsed time is used.
questions.modelAnswer: Horizontal acceleration is zero; horizontal velocity stays 16.0 m s⁻¹. Vertically, displacement −45.0 m = ½(−9.81)t², giving t = √(90.0/9.81) = 3.03 s. Horizontal distance = 16.0 × 3.03 = 48.5 m. Vertical impact velocity = −gt = −29.7 m s⁻¹. Impact speed = √(16.0² + 29.7²) = 33.7 m s⁻¹ approximately. Horizontal and vertical motion occur simultaneously, so the same elapsed time is used.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 mock application 4
questions.subtopic: Area and stiffness from a piecewise-linear force–extension plot
questions.prompt: A force–extension graph joins (extension 0.000 m, force 0 N), (0.040 m, 80 N) and (0.080 m, 110 N) using straight line segments. Determine the initial stiffness, the work done to extend to 0.040 m and to 0.080 m, and explain why extrapolating the first segment's stiffness to 0.080 m is inappropriate.
markPoints: Initial stiffness is the initial force–extension gradient.
Area from 0 to 0.040 m is ½ × 80 × 0.040 = 1.60 J.
Total work done to 0.080 m is 1.60 + 3.80 = 5.40 J.
The second segment has a different gradient so stiffness is not constant across the full range.
questions.modelAnswer: Initial stiffness is the initial force–extension gradient. k = 80 N / 0.040 m = 2000 N m⁻¹. Area from 0 to 0.040 m is ½ × 80 × 0.040 = 1.60 J. Area from 0.040 to 0.080 m is ½(80 + 110) × 0.040 = 3.80 J. Total work done to 0.080 m is 1.60 + 3.80 = 5.40 J. The second segment has a different gradient so stiffness is not constant across the full range.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 mock application 5
questions.subtopic: Experimental V–I graph with lost volts
questions.prompt: Measurements for a cell give terminal p.d. V=1.60 V at I=0 A, V=1.40 V at I=0.50 A and V=1.20 V at I=1.00 A. Treat the graph V against I as a straight line. Determine emf, internal resistance, lost volts and terminal p.d. at 1.00 A; explain the meaning of the negative graph gradient.
markPoints: The V-axis intercept at zero current gives emf ε = 1.60 V.
The internal resistance is r = 0.40 Ω, the magnitude of the negative gradient.
Lost volts at 1.00 A are Ir = 1.00 × 0.40 = 0.40 V.
Terminal p.d. at 1.00 A is ε − Ir = 1.20 V.
The negative gradient shows increasing current causes greater internal voltage drop and hence smaller terminal p.d.
questions.modelAnswer: The V-axis intercept at zero current gives emf ε = 1.60 V. The gradient ΔV/ΔI = (1.20 − 1.60)/(1.00 − 0) = −0.40 V A⁻¹. The internal resistance is r = 0.40 Ω, the magnitude of the negative gradient. Lost volts at 1.00 A are Ir = 1.00 × 0.40 = 0.40 V. Terminal p.d. at 1.00 A is ε − Ir = 1.20 V. The negative gradient shows increasing current causes greater internal voltage drop and hence smaller terminal p.d.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 mock application 6
questions.subtopic: Finite load changes a potential divider output
questions.prompt: A 12.0 V ideal supply is connected to a potential divider with a 2.0 kΩ upper resistor and a 4.0 kΩ lower resistor. Output is measured across the lower resistor. A 4.0 kΩ load is then connected in parallel with the lower resistor. Calculate the unloaded output, loaded effective lower resistance and loaded output. Explain the change.
markPoints: The load is parallel with the lower 4.0 kΩ resistor.
The effective lower resistance is 1/(1/4.0 + 1/4.0) = 2.0 kΩ.
With a smaller lower-branch resistance, a smaller fraction of the 12.0 V supply appears across it.
questions.modelAnswer: Unloaded output = 12.0 × 4.0/(2.0+4.0) = 8.0 V. The load is parallel with the lower 4.0 kΩ resistor. The effective lower resistance is 1/(1/4.0 + 1/4.0) = 2.0 kΩ. Loaded output = 12.0 × 2.0/(2.0+2.0) = 6.0 V. The output falls by 2.0 V. With a smaller lower-branch resistance, a smaller fraction of the 12.0 V supply appears across it.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Year 1 mock application 7
questions.prompt: Two liquids, straight-chain hexane and 2,2-dimethylbutane, both have formula C₆H₁₄. Hexane has the higher boiling point. Explain why, referring to structure and intermolecular forces. Explain why a claim that hexane has more electrons is incorrect.
markPoints: The two substances have the same molecular formula, C₆H₁₄.
They therefore have the same total number of electrons per molecule.
Hexane has a less branched, more extended molecular shape.
Its molecules can generally achieve greater contact surface area with neighbours.
This tends to strengthen induced dipole–dipole (London/van der Waals') forces and increase hexane's boiling point.
questions.modelAnswer: The two substances have the same molecular formula, C₆H₁₄. They therefore have the same total number of electrons per molecule. Hexane has a less branched, more extended molecular shape. Its molecules can generally achieve greater contact surface area with neighbours. This tends to strengthen induced dipole–dipole (London/van der Waals') forces and increase hexane's boiling point.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Year 1 mock application 8
questions.prompt: Use the supplied mean bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C=C 612; C–C 347; C–H 413; H–H 436. For the conceptual reaction C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆, estimate ΔH using bonds broken minus bonds formed. Explain why a result using mean bond enthalpies is approximate.
markPoints: One C=C bond and one H–H bond are broken in the net change.
Energy for bonds broken = 612 + 436 = 1048 kJ mol⁻¹.
One C–C bond and two additional C–H bonds form.
Energy released by bonds formed = 347 + 2(413) = 1173 kJ mol⁻¹.
Mean bond enthalpies are average gaseous-bond values and are approximate for particular molecules.
questions.modelAnswer: One C=C bond and one H–H bond are broken in the net change. Energy for bonds broken = 612 + 436 = 1048 kJ mol⁻¹. One C–C bond and two additional C–H bonds form. Energy released by bonds formed = 347 + 2(413) = 1173 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH = 1048 − 1173 = −125 kJ mol⁻¹. Mean bond enthalpies are average gaseous-bond values and are approximate for particular molecules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Year 1 mock application 9
questions.subtopic: Correct a calorimetry cooling curve by extrapolation
questions.prompt: In an illustrative calorimetry data exercise, mixing occurs at t=60 s. The original mixture temperature is 20.0 °C; after the reaction, the cooling-line readings are 38.0 °C at 120 s and 36.6 °C at 180 s. Treat cooling as linear over this interval. Find the corrected maximum temperature at t=60 s and calculate ΔH when 50.0 g solution (c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹) absorbed heat from 0.100 mol of reaction. Explain why extrapolation is used.
markPoints: Extrapolation backwards 60 s to mixing time gives corrected maximum = 38.0 + 1.4 = 39.4 °C.
Heat gained by solution q=mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 19.4 = 4054.6 J.
Extrapolation compensates for heat exchange with surroundings before the maximum can be measured directly.
questions.modelAnswer: Cooling rate = (36.6 − 38.0)/(180 − 120) = −0.0233 °C s⁻¹. Extrapolation backwards 60 s to mixing time gives corrected maximum = 38.0 + 1.4 = 39.4 °C. Corrected temperature rise = 39.4 − 20.0 = 19.4 K. Heat gained by solution q=mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 19.4 = 4054.6 J. Convert q to 4.0546 kJ. ΔH per 0.100 mol = −4.0546/0.100 = −40.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (3 s.f.). Extrapolation compensates for heat exchange with surroundings before the maximum can be measured directly.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 Physics mock application 1
questions.prompt: A ball of mass 0.80 kg falls through air. At one instant, the upward air resistance is 3.0 N. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate its weight, resultant force and acceleration. Explain how its acceleration changes as its speed increases, and state the air-resistance force at terminal speed.
markPoints: Resultant force at the specified instant = 7.84 − 3.0 = 4.84 N, downwards.
Air resistance generally increases as speed increases.
The resultant downward force therefore decreases.
The downward acceleration decreases towards zero.
At terminal speed, air resistance balances the weight, 7.84 N; resultant force and acceleration are zero.
questions.modelAnswer: Weight = mg = 0.80 × 9.8 = 7.84 N, downwards. Resultant force at the specified instant = 7.84 − 3.0 = 4.84 N, downwards. Acceleration = 4.84/0.80 = 6.05 m s⁻², downwards. Air resistance generally increases as speed increases. The resultant downward force therefore decreases. The downward acceleration decreases towards zero. At terminal speed, air resistance balances the weight, 7.84 N; resultant force and acceleration are zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 Physics mock application 2
questions.subtopic: Breaking stress versus maximum stress; Young modulus
questions.prompt: A wire initially has uniform cross-sectional area 2.0 mm². During a tensile test, the largest force reached is 550 N, but the wire finally breaks under a force of 500 N. Calculate its breaking stress and its maximum tensile stress. Explain the distinction. In a separate elastic measurement on the same material, a wire 1.0 m long and of the same area extends by 1.0 mm under 100 N. Calculate the Young modulus.
markPoints: Breaking stress is the stress at fracture, which may be lower than the greatest stress sustained earlier.
questions.modelAnswer: Original cross-sectional area = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². Breaking stress = 500/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.50 × 10⁸ Pa. Maximum tensile stress = 550/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.75 × 10⁸ Pa. Breaking stress is the stress at fracture, which may be lower than the greatest stress sustained earlier. Elastic tensile strain = (1.0 × 10⁻³)/1.0 = 1.0 × 10⁻³. Elastic tensile stress = 100/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 5.0 × 10⁷ Pa. Young modulus = stress/strain = (5.0 × 10⁷)/(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 5.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 Physics mock application 3
questions.subtopic: Variable force graph, energy conservation and instantaneous power
questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg trolley starts from rest on a straight horizontal track with negligible resistance. A driving force rises linearly from 10 N at displacement 0 m to 30 N at displacement 4.0 m, then remains 30 N to displacement 6.0 m. Calculate the total work done, the trolley's final speed and the instantaneous power supplied by the force at the 6.0 m point.
markPoints: Work in the first 4.0 m is the trapezium area under the force–displacement graph = ½(10 + 30) × 4.0 = 80 J.
Work from 4.0 m to 6.0 m is the rectangle area = 30 × 2.0 = 60 J.
With negligible resistive loss, work becomes kinetic energy: ½mv² = 140 J.
Instantaneous power at 6.0 m is P = Fv = 30 × √140 = 355 W (3 s.f.).
questions.modelAnswer: Work in the first 4.0 m is the trapezium area under the force–displacement graph = ½(10 + 30) × 4.0 = 80 J. Work from 4.0 m to 6.0 m is the rectangle area = 30 × 2.0 = 60 J. Total work done = 80 + 60 = 140 J. With negligible resistive loss, work becomes kinetic energy: ½mv² = 140 J. Final speed v = √(2 × 140 / 2.0) = √140 = 11.8 m s⁻¹ (3 s.f.). Instantaneous power at 6.0 m is P = Fv = 30 × √140 = 355 W (3 s.f.).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 Electricity mock application 1
questions.subtopic: Identical cells in series with internal resistance
questions.prompt: Three identical cells, each with emf 1.50 V and internal resistance 0.20 Ω, are connected in series to a 4.5 Ω external resistor. Calculate the combined emf and internal resistance, the total circuit resistance, the current, the terminal p.d. across the external resistor and the lost volts.
markPoints: Terminal p.d. across the resistor = IR = 0.88235 × 4.5 = 3.97 V (3 s.f.).
Lost volts = Ir = 0.88235 × 0.60 = 0.529 V; terminal p.d. plus lost volts equals emf.
questions.modelAnswer: Combined emf = 3 × 1.50 = 4.50 V. Combined internal resistance = 3 × 0.20 = 0.60 Ω. Total resistance = 4.5 + 0.60 = 5.10 Ω. Current = 4.50/5.10 = 0.882 A (3 s.f.). Terminal p.d. across the resistor = IR = 0.88235 × 4.5 = 3.97 V (3 s.f.). Lost volts = Ir = 0.88235 × 0.60 = 0.529 V; terminal p.d. plus lost volts equals emf.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 Electricity mock application 2
questions.prompt: Two identical cells each have emf 1.50 V and internal resistance 0.60 Ω. They power a 6.0 Ω external resistor, first connected in parallel and then in series. For each arrangement calculate combined emf, combined internal resistance and current. Compare the terminal p.d.s across the resistor and explain why they differ.
markPoints: Parallel arrangement has emf 1.50 V, the same as one cell.
Terminal p.d.s across the resistor: parallel ≈ 1.43 V, series = 2.50 V; the larger series emf gives a larger p.d. here despite increased internal resistance.
questions.modelAnswer: Parallel arrangement has emf 1.50 V, the same as one cell. Parallel internal resistance = 0.60/2 = 0.30 Ω. Parallel current = 1.50/(6.0 + 0.30) = 0.238 A (3 s.f.). Series arrangement has emf = 2 × 1.50 = 3.00 V. Series internal resistance = 2 × 0.60 = 1.20 Ω. Series current = 3.00/(6.0 + 1.20) = 0.417 A (3 s.f.). Terminal p.d.s across the resistor: parallel ≈ 1.43 V, series = 2.50 V; the larger series emf gives a larger p.d. here despite increased internal resistance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 Electricity mock application 3
questions.prompt: A 12.0 V supply is connected across a 4.0 kΩ upper resistor in series with a 2.0 kΩ NTC thermistor as the lower resistor. Output p.d. is measured across the thermistor. Calculate the unloaded output. A 2.0 kΩ load is then connected in parallel with the thermistor. Calculate the loaded output and explain qualitatively what happens to the loaded output if the thermistor temperature rises.
markPoints: Before loading, total series resistance = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 kΩ.
Loaded lower branch effective resistance = (2.0 × 2.0)/(2.0 + 2.0) = 1.0 kΩ.
An NTC thermistor's resistance decreases as temperature rises.
As its resistance falls, lower-branch effective resistance and its fraction of supply p.d. decrease, so loaded output falls.
questions.modelAnswer: Before loading, total series resistance = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 kΩ. Unloaded output = 12.0 × 2.0/6.0 = 4.0 V. Loaded lower branch effective resistance = (2.0 × 2.0)/(2.0 + 2.0) = 1.0 kΩ. Loaded output = 12.0 × 1.0/(4.0 + 1.0) = 2.4 V. An NTC thermistor's resistance decreases as temperature rises. As its resistance falls, lower-branch effective resistance and its fraction of supply p.d. decrease, so loaded output falls.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 Waves mock application 1
questions.prompt: A uniform string is fixed at both ends with vibrating length 0.80 m, mass per unit length 0.50 g m⁻¹ and tension 80 N. Calculate the wave speed, wavelength and frequency of its first harmonic. Calculate the wavelength and frequency of its third harmonic, then determine the first-harmonic frequency if tension is reduced to 20 N while length and mass per unit length stay unchanged.
markPoints: Mass per unit length = 0.50 g m⁻¹ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹.
With tension reduced from 80 N to 20 N, speed and first-harmonic frequency halve, so f₁ becomes 125 Hz.
questions.modelAnswer: Mass per unit length = 0.50 g m⁻¹ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹. Wave speed = √(80/(5.0 × 10⁻⁴)) = 400 m s⁻¹. First-harmonic wavelength = 2 × 0.80 = 1.60 m. First-harmonic frequency = v/λ = 400/1.60 = 250 Hz. Third-harmonic wavelength = 2L/3 = 0.533 m. Third-harmonic frequency = 3 × 250 = 750 Hz. With tension reduced from 80 N to 20 N, speed and first-harmonic frequency halve, so f₁ becomes 125 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 Waves mock application 2
questions.subtopic: Young double-slit spacing and white light
questions.prompt: In Young's double-slit experiment, monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm passes through slits separated by 0.30 mm. A screen is 2.0 m away. Calculate the fringe spacing and the distance spanning eight consecutive fringe intervals. State the effect on fringe spacing if the slit separation doubles. If white light is used instead, explain why the central fringe is white and which colour has fringes further from the centre.
markPoints: Convert wavelength 600 nm = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m and slit separation 0.30 mm = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Eight consecutive fringe intervals span 8 × 4.0 = 32 mm.
If slit separation doubles, fringe spacing halves to 2.0 mm.
With white light, the centre is white because path difference there is zero for all wavelengths.
Outside the centre, longer-wavelength red fringes lie further out than shorter-wavelength blue/violet fringes.
questions.modelAnswer: Convert wavelength 600 nm = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m and slit separation 0.30 mm = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m. Fringe spacing w = λD/s = (6.0 × 10⁻⁷ × 2.0)/(3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.0040 m = 4.0 mm. Eight consecutive fringe intervals span 8 × 4.0 = 32 mm. If slit separation doubles, fringe spacing halves to 2.0 mm. With white light, the centre is white because path difference there is zero for all wavelengths. Outside the centre, longer-wavelength red fringes lie further out than shorter-wavelength blue/violet fringes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Year 1 Waves mock application 3
questions.subtopic: Optical fibre critical angle and signal quality
questions.prompt: An optical fibre has a core refractive index of 1.50 and cladding refractive index of 1.46. Calculate the critical angle at their boundary. State whether a ray in the core incident at 79.0° to the normal undergoes total internal reflection, explaining why. Distinguish modal from material dispersion, explain how pulse broadening limits the data rate, and state the effect of absorption on the signal.
markPoints: At the core–cladding boundary, sin θc = ncladding/ncore = 1.46/1.50.
Critical angle θc ≈ 76.7° measured from the normal.
At 79.0° incidence, total internal reflection occurs since light travels from higher to lower refractive index and 79.0° is greater than θc.
Modal dispersion is pulse spreading because rays follow paths of different lengths in a step-index fibre.
Material dispersion is pulse spreading because different wavelengths travel at different speeds in the fibre.
Pulse broadening can cause neighbouring digital pulses to overlap, limiting data rate.
Absorption transfers light energy to the fibre material, reducing optical signal intensity.
questions.modelAnswer: At the core–cladding boundary, sin θc = ncladding/ncore = 1.46/1.50. Critical angle θc ≈ 76.7° measured from the normal. At 79.0° incidence, total internal reflection occurs since light travels from higher to lower refractive index and 79.0° is greater than θc. Modal dispersion is pulse spreading because rays follow paths of different lengths in a step-index fibre. Material dispersion is pulse spreading because different wavelengths travel at different speeds in the fibre. Pulse broadening can cause neighbouring digital pulses to overlap, limiting data rate. Absorption transfers light energy to the fibre material, reducing optical signal intensity.
